speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In his address to the National Pensions Conference in March, 1981, the Prime Minister said:
February 9. 1982

We are determined to bring about a substantial pension reform-that determination imposes a sense of urgency.
The Prime Minister then promised a July meeting with the provinces on pensions. We have had no such meeting. The government then promised a green paper on pensions for October. We have had no such green paper. October became December, December became February, and now we are told that we should expect it in May, and the paper is no longer green. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright):
That this House censure the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, all of whom were participants in the National Pensions Conference held in Ottawa last March, for their irresponsible delay in failing to provide adequate or any solution to the urgent and pressing needs of pensioners in Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to come back to the question of the split in the government over the budget, and I would address my question to the Prime Minister who will recall, I am sure, the classic definition of cabinet solidarity as given by the late Prime Minister Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the occasion of his firing of the minister, Israel Tarte, from his cabinet over a disagreement on tariff policy. Mr. Laurier said at that time, in 1903:
it would be a mere redundancy for me to affirm that the necessity for solidarity between the members of the same administration is absolute; that the moment a policy has been determined upon, then it becomes the duty of every member of that administration to support it and to support it in its entirety.
That was Prime Minister Laurier's standard, and it has been the standard of all Prime Ministers to this date. Does the Prime Minister accept that definition of cabinet solidarity?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am satisfied that the caucus is entirely behind the Minister of Finance in this matter.

For all these reasons, I believe that we must resist the temptation to veer away from restraint, whether to gain a temporary and minimal increase in jobs or simply to reap the transitory political benefits.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, as the Prime Minister did when he described hon. members of Parliament as nobodies, and as he did when he muzzled this House, he now proposes to joke about the fundamental traditions of our Parliament as he ignores them. Our interest here is not in quoting Laurier; rather, our interest here is to ensure that respect is given to what Laurier stood for and what every Prime Minister before this Prime Minister stood for in terms of cabinet solidarity.

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING FREEDOM OF MINISTERS TO DISAGREE ON POLICY

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING FREEDOM OF MINISTERS TO DISAGREE ON POLICY
speechtext: I would like to make the very loose standards which the country has come to associate with this Prime Minister exactly clear. That is what the Minister of National Health and Welfare has done. That is what the Minister of State has done. If that is the standard of the Prime Minister, let him say so; if it is not, let him tell us his standard of cabinet solidarity.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at last!
I have a question for the Prime Minister. Does the Prime Minister agree that one of the original purposes of the Crow rate was to encourage the establishment and maintenance of rural communities on the prairies and, if so, does he realize that the proposal made by the Minister of Transport in Winnipeg yesterday could have exactly the opposite effect if implemented, namely, the destruction of those communities?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-PURPOSE OF ESTABLISHMENT AND CONSEQUENCE OF CHANGE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Crow rate was established in order to encourage the development of agriculture in the west. Of course included in that is the establishment of a solid economic base for many communities in the west.
There have been some changes in the country over the last 100 years with regard to methods of transportation, methods of production, the size of our markets, the growth rate of communities, urbanization movements, in demographic movements within Canada, and in changes of the age groups.
After this period of time 1 think it is perfectly reasonable for the government to review something which has existed since the last decade of the nineteenth century, in conjunction with all the interests in the west, and to appoint a westerner, a professor of agriculture and economics in the west, to help bring together the various and sometimes opposing views in the west on how this should be done. That is the position of the government.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the minister responsible for agriculture. Fuel costs under this government have risen 65 cents a gallon. Gasoline costs have gone up 86 cents a gallon under this government's administration. Machine costs have gone up 100 per cent in the last three years. Facing these increased costs to farmers, in the minister's judgment is it fair to put the increased cost of freight on the farmers at this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-EFFECT OF CHANGE ON FARMERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member makes far-reaching statements before he asks his question. I would just answer in this way, when he talks about fuel. The farmers in Canada have fuel much cheaper here than the farmers in the United States of America. They are still better off than the main farmers with whom they compete.
The hon. member asks is it fair. I believe that in 1970 farmers were paying about 70 per cent of the cost of transportation of their grain at that time. They will be paying by 1985 about 20 per cent or around that Figure; and by 1990 they will be paying about 7 per cent of the cost. The many farmers whom I have talked to have said, "Look, give us a good transportation system; we are willing to pay more for it." We are not suggesting that they pay the full cost of transportation, we are suggesting that they contribute more to the cost of moving their produce.
The minister has just stated that by moving that grain to market, rather then having it in storage on farms or in elevators, we can show by just a 10 per cent improvement there will be $400 million more into the farmers' pockets in western Canada. That is what it is all about, making that economy stronger, making it work better and in a better fashion for all people concerned.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. Given the fact that since the minister spoke, the new unemployment figures are out, that for the first time since the 1930s we have more than one million unemployed, the ten provincial premiers, and Liberal members of Parliament from Quebec and, we understand, some of the Ontario Liberal members, have called on him to take steps now to stimulate the economy and to start reducing the number of unemployed, I wonder if the minister could indicate whether he is giving serious consideration to doing something now rather than waiting six months?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER TAKE EARLY ACTION TO HELP REDUCE UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am not aware of using the expression "six months" in my Toronto speech. What I did say was that I could not at the present time contemplate a major stimulant of the economy. I listed the reasons why I thought it would not be the best way to create jobs in Canada, that what we might do now we would lose later on. But I said that within the policy of restraint I was quite prepared to state that the government would consider taking targeted and specific measures to improve growth, productivity and investment. 1 believe that the comments made by my caucus colleagues were perfectly consistent with the particular approach I laid out in that speech.

one million unemployed according to Statistics Canada, there are also 400,000 or 500,000 people who have not been counted because they have quit looking for work. How long will we have to wait? How much more unemployment will we have before the minister realizes that his policies are leading to further disaster? Will we receive policies to create jobs rather than to destroy them?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It is a follow-up to a question which I asked him last year with respect to the serious crisis faced in the forest industry with lay-offs of over 100,000 people throughout Canada. I was delighted to hear yesterday that he followed my suggestion that idle hands in the forest industry should be used in the task of forest renewal and in its various areas. How many agreements has the minister signed with provinces? Is it the intention of the federal government to go into partnership directly with industry to ensure that the gap is bridged, that some of these people retain their jobs, and that in so doing we make a long-term investment in our future, namely, the replenishment and renewal of our depleting forestry resources?

Madam Speaker, at this point in time the agreement we signed with Ontario is the only one. It is based upon the proposal to put several thousand workers back into Ontario forests. At the time of the announcement 1 also indicated that that particular arrangement is available to all other provincial governments which have major forest industries within their jurisdiction. I will be writing to the provincial ministers of those provinces to outline the details and criterion of the program. In the hon. member's province of British Columbia there has already been some initial indication of interest. Certainly I welcome his help in developing a program for that province, as I would in any other province.
At the same time we have available for the forest industry the work-sharing concept, which means that forestry companies would be able to maintain part of their work force under a work-sharing arrangement. We would deal directly with the companies and the unions in that respect. I would certainly
welcome any help the hon. member would give in working with the companies and the provincial governments in this area. I would be quite happy to speak with him after question period so that we can work out arrangements.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, as I understand it, the minister is relying solely upon the resources of the unemployment insurance fund to sustain these new programs. Is there any additional money at his disposal to further the aims of what he announced?

Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-CONCEPT OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY OF CABINET
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a far more serious and important question of privilege.

subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-CONCEPT OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY OF CABINET
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-CONCEPT OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY OF CABINET
speechtext: I hear the jeers of Liberal hecklers across the way before they even know the nature of my question of privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-CONCEPT OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY OF CABINET
speechtext: I said "Let's hear it".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-CONCEPT OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY OF CABINET
speechtext:
The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) is one of the hecklers. I rise not only as a member of the House to make this appeal on behalf of
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
every individual member and all members collectively, but as one of the officers of the House who has an obligation and a responsibility to see to it that the constitutional conventions of this place remain intact, indeed that the institution itself is not eroded.
It concerns a very valid distinction which must be made between the concept of cabinet solidarity and collective responsibility. In the former case it is a political question. The splits and the cracks as they show might entertain us, but do not suggest themselves as a remedy on a question of privilege. But the latter principle of collective responsibility strikes at the very heart of the reason for being in this place.
I have only had the opportunity since the matter arose during this question period to provide myself with three precedents which I will submit to the Chair for consideration in a moment.
Collective responsibility, which is not what was being spoken of today in the exchanges but was the subject matter of the exchange, is a concept which legitimizes the position and advantages possessed by the ministry in this House, being responsible government. It strikes at the very roots of responsible government. Responsible government, the foundation of our parliamentary democracy, holds that the ministry must have the support of the majority of the House of Commons to carry out the functions of the administration. I will be citing from Sir W. Ivor Jennings in that light in a moment or two.
Collective responsibility, in my submission, Madam Speaker, recognizes that each of the members of the ministry draws his or her personal mandate from majority support given by the House to the cabinet as a whole. If a cabinet minister, and the authorities are clear on this point, tries to put distance between the cabinet's stated policy and his or her own public declarations, then that person puts himself or herself and the House of Commons in a false position, which the House has a right to see resolved.
In my submission, the cabinet is collectively responsible to the House of Commons for the development of policy and the administration of the government. This responsibility is confirmed in a series of votes held throughout the parliamentary year, most notably the Speech from the Throne, on opposition no-confidence motions and on the budget votes, which we have already taken in this House. It is because the present government has carried the House and its members with it on these votes that it is entitled to carry on as a ministry.
Each individual minister draws his or her own position, authority and privileges as a cabinet minister from the acceptance by the House of the policies of the government. Ministers are accorded by the House the right to answer questions, to table documents, to move certain motions and to speak at times for extended periods. They have larger offices and staff allocations. Flowing from this position in the House ministers are able to exercise executive direction over their departments.
If a minister publicly expresses disagreement with a key element of government economic policy by putting forward the

February 9, 1982
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
idea that short-term economic stimulation is not antithetical to the long-term battle against inflation, then he or she is directly opposing the stated view of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and is attacking a policy approved by the House when it supported the finance minister's budget.
The two ministers are thereby challenging their own right to continue as ministers because they are challenging the policy by reason of which the House has confirmed the government's mandate as a government. Members of the House are therefore entitled to ask, how do these two members of cabinet justify their continued exercise of the rights and privileges of a cabinet minister when they themselves have rejected the policies on the basis of which the House has allowed them these rights and privileges?
Logically, Madam Speaker, and in constitutional practice, there are only two conclusions that may be drawn. Either the two ministers feel that the House does not in fact still support the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and, therefore, it is the rest of the cabinet, and not themselves, which is ignoring the will of the House. Or the two ministers who signed the letter have chosen to disagree with the policy still supported by this House, and consequently must resign the positions and privileges accorded to those who accept the implications of collective responsibility.
I submit that this interpretation is the normal and obvious one. It is supported by two quotations, one from Laundy and Phillips in "An Encyclopedia of Parliament". The other is from Redlich's "The Procedure of the House of Commons".
Because the House allows specific privileges to ministers and because the majority in the House has supported the cabinet in certain of its policies, cabinet ministers who will not support these policies have an obligation to the House to resign. That is a paraphrase from page xiii of Redlich's "The Procedure of the House of Commons."
As the spokesman of the House to the Crown, I submit that you have an obligation to assist the House in resolving the invidious position in which this House and all of its members have been placed by this utter disregard of the principle upon which the institution itself has been founded, namely, the principle of collective responsibility. Nothing could be clearer from the two references which I have referred to you for your consideration.
In "An Encyclopedia of Parliament", the pages for reference are numbers 66 and 67. I will quote briefly from the bottom of page 66 as follows:
The cabinet is thus a committee drawn from the ministers of the government, presided over by the Prime Minister, whose function is to frame the general policy of the government and to co-ordinate its administrative activities. It accepts collective responsibility for all the activities of the government, from which it follows that there must be no fundamental disagreement amongst its members.
Further on in the same paragraph, we find this:
Every minister must abide by cabinet decisions or resign, and an attack upon an individual minister is an attack on the cabinet as a whole.
Cabinet proceedings are then described, and so on.
I have one last quotation for the attention of the Chair from Sir W. Ivor Jennings. It is found in the third edition of "Cabinet Government". I do not think there can be any doubt about the standing of Sir Ivor Jennings as an authority. No one would quarrel with him. Here is what Sir Ivor Jennings says about cabinet responsibility, since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does not seem to like the word "Solidarity". At page 277 of the third edition, Jennings quotes Lord Salisbury as follows:
It is only on the principle that absolute responsibility is undertaken by every member of the cabinet who, after a decision is arrived at. remains a member of it. that the joint responsibility of ministers to Parliament can be upheld, and one of the most essential principles of parliamentary responsibility be established.
In other words, the collective responsibility of cabinet for everything that is done is one of the most essential principles of parliamentary responsibility.
If we are to allow this, Madam Speaker-and I urge upon you the responsibility which you, in my submission, have for the protection of the rights of all of us in this institution-and if you will not assist in helping us to resolve this issue, then the government will continue this invidious practice and the whole concept of collective responsibility falls to the ground, much to the ultimately disastrous consequence of the usefulness of this institution.

I therefore very strongly suggest, Madam Speaker, that you take the matter under advisement, consider the references I have cited, and if you should indeed find there is a very vital question of privilege involved here, collectively and individually, then I would move the appropriate motion to have the whole question examined in the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections in the hope they could report at the earliest possible moment in order that there be no further erosion of a long accepted principle, one which is so vitally important to the continued function of this institution.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. NIELSEN-CONCEPT OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY OF CABINET
speechtext:
In response to the hon. member, to begin with it was not clear to me whether this question of privilege really arose directly out of today's deliberations, but I listened anyway. There were questions asked about the matter of cabinet solidarity so I assumed that this question flowed from today's deliberations, which is why I listened to the hon. member, although he was referring to something which happened outside the House and might have required notice. I just want to point that out to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) because he did not say quite clearly for what reason he was rising at this moment to invoke his question of privilege.
If the hon. member looks at the definition of a question of privilege, and I am sure he has looked at it nearly as often as 1 have, he will see that he has not demonstrated to me in any way that he was subjected to any type of harassment, threat or any other impediment which might have founded his question of privilege. He refers to cabinet authority as emanating from this institution. I must reply that these matters concern ethics, and if ministers are to be more or less in solidarity with
February 9, 1982

government policies, that is a choice they themselves make. It has very much to do with their personal conception of ethics.
As for what the Prime Minister's conduct should be in these cases, that also refers to any Prime Minister's personal concept of ethics and to the importance that he attaches to the way cabinet solidarity should be expressed. I can see the hon. member does not agree with the Prime Minister's concept of cabinet solidarity. That is his choice and his privilege, of course, and he may dispute it as much as he cares to. I am sure he will not let any occasion pass by where he can express his sentiments on this particular matter.
Throughout the history of Canada I suppose we have had several types of cabinet and several types of expressions of cabinet solidarity, and that these cabinets have been more or less efficient, related or not to the way in which they dealt with cabinet solidarity. I guess this is what makes for the strength or weakness of cabinets, but I fail to see it as the foundation for a question of privilege, be it individual or collective. I do not see how we can consider a collective question of privilege because it is defined as relating to an individual member.
However, the hon. member has invoked a personal privilege so I can answer him. Despite the pleas the hon. member makes to me to assist the House in obtaining redress on what he feels is a question of privilege, I must say I cannot assist him in obtaining this redress. This is the kind of thing that parties in the House dispute and debate at length, and I invite them to do just that on the proper occasion.
The hon. member has quoted many authorities, all extremely remarkable, and it was interesting to hear these quotations and refresh our memories about some of the principles which form the basis of cabinet solidarity, which is more a custom than anything else. However, he has not demonstrated to me where his privilege was affected in this particular circumstance; therefore, I must tell him that I cannot find a prima facie case of privilege.

UNDUE LENGTH OF QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order arising out of some remarks you made today during question period. I rise to support and encourage you in what you said to us at that time. I believe this affects all of us here, and indeed affects the function of the institution of Parliament itself.
My point of order has to do with the length of some questions and answers in question period. I blame no particular person, but this afternoon it just happened to be the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in an exchange which took some 15 minutes and gobbled up the time of other members. I just thought it was important that some of us rise and say that we will support and encourage you to try to police question period as much as possible.
Point of Order-Mr. Nystrom
In doing that 1 want to refer you to Beauchesne's filth edition, page 131, Section 358(2), where it says:
Answers to questions should be as brief as possible-
I think, Madam Speaker, after watching the Prime Minister in particular today, that the answers were very long indeed. In addition, I would refer you to Section 359 of Beauchesne's, where it says:
A brief question seeking information-
The words are "brief question". It goes on to say:
(1)	It must be a question, not an expression of an opinion, representation, argumentation, nor debate.
(2)	The question must be brief. A preamble need not exceed one carefully drawn sentence. A long preamble on a long question takes an unfair share of time and provokes the same sort of reply. A supplementary question should need no preamble.
I point this out, Madam Speaker, because there are 284 members in this House. All of us are politicians, all of us can be very verbose, and if we let this trend continue there is going to be less and less participation from all of us in this House.
I make these remarks in a totally non-partisan manner because we can all be as guilty as the next person. I just wanted to encourage you to do what you can to make question period a bit more snappy and functional, which in turn will make Parliament a bit more meaningful for the people of Canada.

what the Prime Minister is up to when he stands in the House and takes up all of our time. He realizes that there are a few million TV viewers out there and that the more TV time he gets, the better he will appear. That is the real purpose behind what he does.

Concerning the shortness or length of questions and answers, I do want to remind the hon. members that, as I do with regard to questions, I occasionally rise in an attempt to get hon. members to terminate their answers.

subtopic: UNDUE LENGTH OF QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
speechtext: Very occasionally.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: UNDUE LENGTH OF QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
speechtext:
If one looks at Hansard, one finds that that is substantiated. However, I think hon. members are overlooking the fact that the Chair is here every day and knows what is happening in the House. I do not pretend to be the only one who knows what is going on in the House, but I do know what is going on. I am here every day; I can judge who is lengthy one day and who has been lengthy for a whole week. From time to time I decide to move in on an hon. member to ask him to be a bit more brief. Perhaps I might have been lenient for two or three days in a row if I felt the hon. member had a point to make; but, then, on the fourth day, I might decide to move in on him because he simply might have thought that I would allow him to carry on in this manner forever.
There are circumstances in which some hon. members must have more time in order to expose their questions, and I try to judge such circumstances as best I can. As I say, I am not always universally correct in my instant judgments, but 1 do my best. I would like the trust of the House with regard to this particular task which, believe me, is not exactly an easy one.
When hon. members do not follow my direction to be shorter in their answers, I do compensate. Hon. members will have noticed today that four Liberals wanted to ask questions, but none of them was allowed. I did not recognize them in compensation for the fact that some of the answers had been rather lengthy. Furthermore, I extended the question period by seven minutes to compensate for the time which had been taken during the question period as a result of heckling and applauding so as not to penalize those hon. members who were very eager to ask questions.
I welcome the remarks of hon. members because 1 hate to stand up here and preach to them every day. I do not conceive my role as being one which tries to prevent people from doing what they want to do, but, on the contrary, one which ensures that the debates are conducted in such a fashion that everyone will have a chance to express themselves. I must make such judgments on a daily basis. I therefore welcome the remarks and the terrific resolve shown by hon. members to ask questions which will be short, snappy and to the point. That would result in a great question period.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order that has to do with this one and concerns the duration of question period. The Standing Orders are also very clear as to the duration of question period, at what time it is supposed to begin and when it is supposed to end. If questions are too long or if members are noisy on either side of the House, I submit that the Speaker of the House is bound by the Standing Orders and has no discretion to extend question period beyond the time set in Standing Order 15(3), which is very specific.
We are prepared to moderate the length of our answers, provided the questions are brief as well. We want to be clear and concise and comprehensive, but on the other hand, we
February 9, 1982

should also appreciate it if the Standing Orders were applied literally, where the duration of question period is concerned. It is not because we are sticklers for form, but because we the ministers, including myself, have other commitments, and our daily schedules are arranged on the assumption that we shall be able to leave at three o'clock and not at 3.07 or 3.09.

As for the remarks by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis), I should like to point out that there are some courtesies the Speaker of the House must observe with regard to the Prime Minister of this country and the Leader of the Opposition. I have my own concept of what these courtesies should be, and I try to be fair and, of course, I must be fair. But there are also days when 1 may decide to laugh along with the hon. members, and I find it is a way of relieving tension in the House. I have noticed that there are members who sometimes object to the fact that I smile from time to time, but I think it is a very healthy attitude for the Speaker not to take life too seriously, and I think that when emotions start rising in the House, the Speaker should remain calm and keep a sense of humour. MOTIONS TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   TRANSPORT PROPOSED CHANGES TO CROWSNEST PASS RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 26, I ask leave of the House to consider a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. It arises out of the announcement made in Winnipeg yesterday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) concerning major changes to the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. The minister chose to make this important announcement outside the House, thereby denying members of the House of Commons the opportunity to respond and to seek clarification of the many complex aspects of the government's proposal.
The announcement, Madam Speaker, proposed to remove an historical and statutory right enjoyed by the grain producers of Canada and will result in an openended freight rate structure which will cost producers hundreds of millions of dollars. This comes at a time when producer costs are rising and incomes declining. Because of the profound effect this policy will have on Canada's grain producers, because Parliament has been circumvented by the minister's announcement, because the policy requires clarification and answers to the many questions it raises, I believe it is imperative that Parliament be allowed to debate this urgent and vital matter.
If you find these conditions consistent with the terms of Standing Order 26, Madam Speaker, I will be prepared to move the appropriate motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Madam Speaker, I have given you the appropriate notice, seconded by the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), to move the adjournment of the House pursuant to Standing Order 26 for the purpose of debating a specific and important motion requiring immediate consideration, namely the government's announcement outside Parliament in Winnipeg yesterday that it is proceeding to abandon the Crowsnest Pass grain rate, the confederation bargain protecting western farmers against the monopoly powers of the railways of this country, which will depress farm, income even further and have serious ramifications on the national economy of Canada.
As you know, Madam Speaker, the rules do not permit me to elaborate on the reasons for moving the motion, except to say that I believe the representatives in this House of the people of the prairies must have an opportunity to have some input into the debate on this very important issue. The Crowsnest rate agreement in western Canada is like the Magna Carta to our part of the country and we need an opportunity to discuss it here in this House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTIONS TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   TRANSPORT PROPOSED CHANGES TO CROWSNEST PASS RATES

These two notices of motions are quite similar in nature, although worded differently. They were examined very closely so as to make a judgment on whether they fulfil the requirements of Standing Order 26.
I need not remind hon. members that since its inception in 1897, the Crowsnest Pass agreement has been the subject over the years of many discussions and debates in the House of Commons. The fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has now announced a change in those rates, a change which will be subject to consultations, studies and even legislation, does not meet the requirements for a debate under Standing Order 26, although I recognize that it is very important to debate this question.
The hon. members who submitted the motions, in my opinion, have not demonstrated clearly and precisely that, in the words of Section 16 of Standing Order 26, the matter proposed for discussion relates to a genuine emergency calling for immediate and urgent consideration. It is my understanding that the Minister of Transport will be introducing legislation respecting the Crowsnest Pass agreement, at which time there will be ample opportunity for debate.
In addition, there are several opposition days remaining in this supply period when hon. members may set down motions to discuss this particular subject. Accordingly, it is with regret that I cannot accept the hon. members' applications.
