speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cosgrove that Bill C-89, to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising today to discuss Bill C-89 which has been introduced by the government. It provides legislative authority to the government for its housing programs and for the implementation of the measures in the November 12 budget dealing with housing. It provides the authority for neighbourhood improvement and public works at the municipal level.
It almost goes without saying that the provisions in this legislation are totally inadequate to meet the housing needs of Canadians and completely fail to provide the economic stimulus needed to provide work for the over one million Canadians who are unemployed today. It is not only Canadians and New Democrats who are aware of these failures to provide economic stimulus; this knowledge is even beginning to penetrate the backbenches of the Liberal caucus. That in itself is an accomplishment because of the reputation the Liberal party has of being a party with discipline.
February 9, 1982

I would like to read from an article in La Presse dated February 8, an article which I think is important for people to be aware of. It reads:

Following two meetings of their regional caucus, the members of Parliament for the central-eastern part of Montreal have released a letter to the Prime Minister asking Mr. Trudeau to immediately initiate measures to fight unemployment.
The first proposal calls for the stimulation of the housing construction
industry because of its well known spin-off effects.
It is extraordinary that Liberal backbenchers would recognize that there is a real need for economic incentives.

The question that we must ask ourselves is, why do the programs of the government, particularly in housing, fall so dismally short of what is needed? Not only do they fall short of people's basic human needs, but they do not provide any help for the general health of the economy.
There are some basic reasons why these programs fall short of what is needed, and I must say that some of these reasons apply equally to the programs of the past Conservative government. I do not wish to leave those hon. members in comfort. Quite simply, this government, as well as past governments, has refused to understand and recognize the value of investing the public dollar, particularly in the area of housing with which we are concerned today. The government is blinded by its preoccupation with deficits. Incidentally, if you consider both federal and provincial revenues, these deficits would come much more into balance.
Not only does the government refuse to recognize the value of investment, but it is also afraid of charting an independent economic policy for Canada. It does not have the courage to establish Canada's own Fiscal policies with its own approach to public expenditures. It does not have the courage to establish our own monetary policies. Of course, this is a well known fact to all Canadians as we watch the government simply follow the actions of the United States government.
There is another important reason why the housing programs of the government do not live up to what is needed. The government does not believe in providing economic leadership. This is clearly what is needed today and it is what Canadians are calling for, including ten Liberal backbenchers. Economic leadership is needed, especially when people are suffering, and it is obvious that Canadians with mortgages are suffering greatly, as well as people who rely on rental accommodation.
Having set out the basic inadequacies of the government housing programs, I would like to deal with them more specifically. First, 1 would like to deal with the mortgage renewal program. I am disappointed that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) is not in the House for this debate. I do not know if he is behind the curtain but I hope he will be here when I deal with some other important matters during my speech.
The minister quite clearly tried to align his mortgage renewal program with the mortgage assistance program established
Housing
by the new Manitoba government. I will not go into detail on this point because my colleague from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) will lay out in detail the differences between those programs later. I will simply say that the federal Liberal program takes the interest which people cannot pay today because of the government's economic policy and rolls it back into the capital debt which these people have in their mortgage. All the government is doing is piling up debt for the future. If this strategy is being applied for the average home owner who is struggling now, in light of the predictions for another rise in interest rates-another ride up the rollercoaster-Canadians surely cannot afford to ride up that rollercoaster again.
The federal program simply protects banks but does nothing to help people. This has forced provincial governments in Manitoba and Saskatchewan to take some real action. I will read to hon. members something printed in an article in The Globe and Mail about the Manitoba program. I point out that it is in The Globe and Mail so that hon. members will know it is not a biased account of the program. The Globe and Mail is hardly a socialist journal, at least not yet. Perhaps with the new New Democratic Party leader in Ontario The Globe and Mail will see the light.
Manitoba's NDP government unveiled a ... interest-relief program yesterday that will put cash into the pockets of needy home owners.
It will not go into the pockets of bankers but into the pockets of home owners.
Home owners whose new mortgage payments exceed 30 per cent of their household income will receive benefits up to $275 a month ... The money doesn't have to be paid back.
The article went on to indicate clearly that any long-term solutions to high interest rates must come from Ottawa. That is where the problem was created. However, clearly there is a difference between the quality and the efficacy of the federal program, which falls far short, and the provincial program in Manitoba, which provides real assistance in the form of real dollars to real people.
Well said.

I want also to draw to the attention of this government the action being taken in Saskatchewan. Manitoba responded with a program. Saskatchewan has responded with legislation and has introduced mortgage moratorium legislation. The Saskatchewan government introduced legislation which will guarantee that no citizen loses his home by virtue of the ever-rising interest rates the government across the way is creating. The federal government clearly could take some legislative action, and the first good move would be to tax the windfall profits of banks and use that money to get some real assistance to people having mortgage difficulties.
I want to refer to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell), who is sitting at my side today. She spoke yesterday about this housing bill, and I must say I was very impressed. Her speech contained a depth of information which

February 9, 1982
Housing
is certainly lacking on the other side of the House. Hon. members opposite do not know how to deal with facts. The hon. member for Vancouver East dealt not only with the mortgage renewal program but also with other important areas of housing.
I dealt with the minister too.
The hon. member dealt with all these things quite well. I am glad the minister is in the House today. 1 welcome him here. I hope he can learn something from this side of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am here to check the facts.

1 am glad the minister is not hiding behind the curtain. The social housing programs this legislation allegedly enables are totally inadequate and, in the words of my colleague, leave one million poor at the mercy of the private sector. My colleague dealt with the program in detail, but that is an accurate evaluation of it. The rental housing program being pursued by the government provides only 15,000 units. It has been said, even by members of the Tory party, that those
15,000	units will not even meet the need in Vancouver. If those rental units were to be built in each community across the country where people rely upon rental units, I doubt there would be one unit for every community in the country. The program is clearly inadequate. Since my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, has dealt in full detail with this aspect of the government's housing programs, I merely point out that they fall short of what is needed, and I will build on what my colleague said and deal with some other aspects of housing.
I intend to deal, for example, with a priority of the minister, native housing. I hope he listens to my comments. I want to deal with the policy, and then perhaps the minister will adjust his policy. I want to deal with native housing, neighbourhood improvement and federal-provincial-municipal financial relationships. These are all matters which I am sure are close to the minister's heart. In his own speech yesterday he said that he places a very high priority on the rural and native housing program. 1 hope his actions will bear out those words. 1 hope to make some comments which might provide him with some perspectives on that program which he might find useful, if he is willing to take action.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I hope you will support the new program.

The rural and native housing program has been around for a decade. It was begun as a result of very heavy lobbying by the Native Council of Canada. The fundamental essence of this program is that it is a native run program. It was native conceived and provides for the needs of native people. The government rightfully plays the role of providing the financial and human resources necessary to support this type of activity, but I must say that the fundamental principle which must underlie this program and its growth and development is the principle that the program be native run. In other words, it must respect the right of self-determination for our
native people. That is a right about which we hear native people speak eloquently and strongly right across the nation. That right is often expressed in relation to nations, but I think it can also apply to communities and government programs. The principles of self-determination and that this program be native run are fundamental. The program has achieved the creation of native housing corporations, but I suggest there is potential for future growth and for strenthening the concept of self determination.
One of the difficulties associated with the present program is that it is subject to two housing bureaucracies. It is subject not just to the federal bureaucracy but also to provincial bureaucracies at the same time. That is because the program is run under a federal-provincial arrangement. In many cases federal-provincial agreements are appropriate, but I suggest such an agreement is inappropriate in relation to native housing corporations. Such corporations should not be subject to two bureaucracies when groups such as co-ops and others who develop housing are involved with only one bureaucracy. Private developers deal essentially with only one housing bureaucracy. I see the minister shaking his head. I ask him to listen carefully: this point is fundamental. It has to do with the fundamental principle underlying the program. It has to do with the fact that only if native people are able to run their own programs will there be any real development of native leadership. That is the only way native people will ever move out of the poverty which has engulfed our communities for the last 100 years.
I believe the first step which must be taken-and it has been taken already-is the creation of native housing corporations. The second step is for the federal government to go it alone in this area and to provide 100 per cent of the money required for native housing so that native people are no longer subject to both federal and provincial bureaucracies. I suggest that would make for a more efficient administrative process. It would deliver a bigger bang for the buck. More housing would be delivered faster because there would be less bureaucracy through which to move.
I would like to look into the future for a moment. I hope the minister has learned something from my previous comments. Once we have only one bureaucracy policing native housing corporations, I suggest the next step should be toward greater and greater responsibility to be held by native housing corporations. This would increase the level of responsibility of native leadership to deal with the real problems of native people. Such an increase in the level of responsibility would increase the strength of the leadership. It would increase its authority and bring about more respect on the part of the native community. This would be beneficial for the whole country.
That is the fundamental principle I see involved in the rural and native housing program, and that principle should be reflected in any projected improvements to the rural and native housing program. I hope there will be improvements. Even if they do not meet my ideals, I would like to see an attempt made to follow these principles.
February 9, 1982
How about more money?

That is exactly what I am talking about. It is not just a question of money, it is how that money is utilized. That is why I just mentioned the principle.
The second aspect of native housing that I would like to deal with is the question of urban native housing. Although it is related to rural native housing to some degree, it is a separate item. Once again we have native housing corporations. They certainly need more money because the native housing corporations under the present program have to rent three units at near market rents in order to be able to subsidize one unit for a moderate income native family. What is left out in this process is the native person who is on low income. If there is anything that a native housing corporation in a city such as Winnipeg or Vancouver or Montreal should do, it is to serve the native people who have the lowest incomes.
1 would like to suggest that there is a necessity here to add dollars to the package to improve the assistance that will allow for the subsidy of rent so that the native housing corporations can serve those native people who have the greatest need, those who have low incomes. This can be done and it is important that it be done. I like to give credit to the federal government for what it does, and I have no objection to that. I have no objection to politicians making great announcements and taking credit.
Give him credit for MURBs.

Here is a real opportunity for him to take unilateral action. The government designed a program which has been around for a decade, one which assumed provincial financial participation. That provincial financial participation has not materialized, but perhaps it is time to learn that that program was in the first instance ill designed. It is time to change the design of the program and for the federal government to go it alone in order to see that no native person in this country will be without adequate housing. I think that is important in the light of the general economic benefit for the native people across the country.
There is one exception with regard to the provinces that I must mention, and that is the province of Saskatchewan, the province of my colleague. The province of Saskatchewan made a commitment for 1,000 units and tied that into the federal program. That is a significant move. So there is an exception. However, I do not want the minister to wait for another ten years to see if another province will move in that direction. I think it is time for him to take some real action which will fill some human need and provide some economic stimulus.
I would like to say something about why it is important to improve the housing conditions of native people in cities, particularly those in poverty conditions. I come from Winnipeg and I think Winnipeg is a good model of what I am thinking about right now. In the inner city of Winnipeg there is unemployment of upwards of 40 per cent, 50 per cent or 60 per cent. There is an old housing stock, and there are native people
Housing
living in the worst kind of housing conditions. When people are living in those kinds of housing conditions, they move around a lot; the children end up going to four or five different schools in one year. One can imagine what a detrimental impact that has on their education.
The teachers in the schools came to me when I was a city councillor in Winnipeg dealing with the question of housing and indicated quite clearly that if those children are going to make use of the dollar that we and the public put into the educational system they must have good, adequate housing and are not living in four or five different locations in the city in one year. How can they get a good education if they have to move every few months? It is just not possible. There is a fundamental issue of justice here.
There is also an economic question here in the sense that if we want to utilize the public dollars that we have invested in education, for example, in order to give people equal opportunity, we must provide them with adequate housing, with good housing, so they can live in one spot, the children can go to one school all year round rather than to five different schools which would put an unnecessary stress and burden on the teachers as well as on the children. Therefore, this matter is essential and important.
I would make one other comment with regard to native housing. I raise this caution to the minister. I hope he listens to what I have to say because I really do feel that perhaps there is some hope that he will act on some of my suggestions, at least partially, and take some remedial action. If I name the principle, perhaps he can at least take a step in the right direction.
I want to caution the minister. I read his news release with regard to the bill we are dealing with today, and a good one it is.
Which is good, the news release or the bill?

He makes reference in this news release to a more businesslike approach. I know that will find much approval in many quarters. He is trying to present a particular public image. Again we have the game of politics. 1 have no objection to anyone playing politics but I do want to caution him, in the application of his ideology, his business-oriented ideology, that he not carry it so far as to impair the potential delivery of programs. In other words, if he applies this notion of making it more businesslike to national housing programs, that he not do it in a way that would make it impossible for native housing corporations to deliver housing.
I just want him to be very careful of how he applies his ideology, to read carefully the recommendations from his own bureaucrats, because he does mention in this same news release "flexibility". He is anxious to have more flexibility. Who is going to have the flexibility? Obviously, it is the bureaucrats. We want to be sure that whatever is being done not be lost in any effort to present a particular kind of public image for the government.

February 9, 1982
Housing
This is just a caution to the minister, a friendly caution, and I hope that as he examines the recommendations from his civil servants he will keep that in mind. I really hope that he will. As he follows his ideology, he could still allow for the program to be workable. That is the important point, in my mind.
So, Mr. Speaker, that is really what I have to say on native housing. I hope the minister takes some recognition of what 1 had to say and that it has some impact on the government's native housing programs and policies. If it does not, I will take note of it and will have something to say here again.
I would like to move on to some other matters that I said I would cover. One of those is the older neighbourhoods. Once again we have the enabling legislation here, which allows the government to get involved in such things as the community services contribution program. That is the program that was to help with the rehabilitation of older neighbourhoods. I wish to share a little information here with the House. The community services contribution program is a program of which the minister last year announced a termination. He still has the gall to continue to issue press releases claiming credit for public works under that program in my province.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am still paying for it.

The minister should not only be paying for it but should be increasing the amount of funds that are available for these municipal public works, in order to provide increased employment across the country and so that the one million people who are unemployed today will have jobs. It is not just a claim for credit for reducing expenditure, for expenditures that are going to end.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Reduced.

Reduced. Let me give the House an example. I do not want to get lost in names, but at one point this program was not called the community services contribution program. Let me quote from the document I have here:
The community services contribution program replaced the municipal infrastructure, municipal incentive and neighbourhood improvement programs.
It replaced three programs.
These 3 programs provided $399 million in loans and grants for 3 kinds of services. The CSCP which began in April of 1980 provided $250 million a year for 10 kinds of services.
They had three programs before they consolidated, they reduced the budget and called it the CSCP and now they are reducing that and soon will be contributing nothing. There has been no assurance from the government side of the House that there will be a replacement program. Bill C-89 enables the government to implement a replacement program, but there is no evidence in the budgetary or expenditure statements of government that it will be replaced. It continues to cut back and to follow its own economic lunacy. The minister should know that there are people in the country who are concerned about the fact that CSCP is being terminated. In fact, many municipal mayors and councillors are concerned. I am sure the minister knows them.
They do not speak to him now.

Shame, indeed. I have a letter from the city of Winnipeg outlining the damage which will result from the termination of the program. I have an inch thick file of letters from towns and cities right across the country. In a letter from the city of Edmonton it was indicated that if the government wanted to show it cared for the west this was the way to do it-institute a replacement program which will aid municipalities in their public works. 1 have a letter from the city of Calgary which indicated its concern about Liberal government cutbacks of funds to local communities. Also I have letters from the Surrey municipal council and the city of Moose Jaw, etc. I have more documentation outlining the genuine concern of Canadians across the country that the program be reinstated and expanded.
Perhaps it is too much to ask of government to institute a replacement program.
What about a replacement government?

That would be ideal, but dealing with the reality of today, the minister should give serious thought to a replacement program. I notice the enabling legislation allows the minister to make loans for neighbourhood improvement and such. At least it is possible for the minister to have a replacement program based upon a loan program that would be in line with his privatization philosophy, if he is not prepared to give grants. He has not indicated a willingness to take that small step. We are waiting for the minister to take seriously the appeals of cities and towns across Canada for funds for municipal public works. The people who are out of work would like to see some dollars for that purpose as well.
I should like to talk briefly about federal-provincial-municipal finance. When the government was first elected Parliament dealt with a bill respecting grants in lieu of taxes. At that time the minister promised, after the legislation went through the House, to study the program put in place. Apparently the study was to be brought before committee so that hon. members could have another look at it. Nothing has happened. The tragedy is that the government continues with a grant in lieu of taxes system, wherein the federal government retains arbitrary authority for how much it will pay for a building located in any municipality when a better model exists and has been put in place. This model is based upon the notion that the federal government respects the local taxation system. We should have a taxation system, rather than a grants system.
In this area there is much to learn from the province of Quebec. There are many hon. members in the House who are from Quebec, so the government has a good source of advice. Quebec implemented a taxation system which respects the local taxation system and local democratic institutions; it is not an arbitrary authoritarian grant program which leaves the final decision with the senior government.
Of course, municipalities are in need of financial resources. The federal government is bloated in terms of financial
February 9, 1982

resources. It should treat fairly local governments as it relates to them in a federal relationship. We know the government has much to learn in the area of intergovernmental relations. I once again flag the fact that the issue is not forgotten. There are municipalities which want the federal government to respect local governments. As well, there are citizens who want the government to respect their locally-elected representatives and to treat them fairly.
In conclusion, all my remarks, whether they relate to this housing legislation, mortgages, social housing, rental housing, native housing, neighbourhood improvement or local municipal finance, are really an appeal to the government to respond to the needs of Canadians. Quite simply they assume a government which is capable of seeing the value of investing in communities and people. They assume a government with the courage to develop Canadian economic policies in the area of monetary and fiscal matters. They assume a government willing to show leadership in economic matters at a time when the people of the country are hurting. They involve a renewed commitment to democracy, not only to political democracy and rights but to economic rights of people. It is time for the government not only to listen but to act.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak on Bill C-89 which was brought in by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Crosgrove) who I am delighted to see present. It amends the National Housing Act and provides very necessary funds. The government says that the proposed legislation would give Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation more flexibility in responding to housing problems and enable it to conduct its operations in a more businesslike manner. I am sure we will all say amen to it and hope it is correct.
I have had dealings with various CMHC offices and certainly in most cases they have been excellent. On other occasions I have not been overly enthused with the delay and doubletalk. In one specific case we were endeavouring to obtain a loan for an apartment house in my home village. We had all the necessary information and approvals. It was getting on to autumn and, just when the entrepreneurs were to commence building, they were told by CMHC that they required special land tests and so on. The upshot was that after spending a few thousand dollars the project involving seven or eight apartments went down the drain.
The plan will offer interest deferral guarantees of up to $3,000 for borrowers who have some equity in their homes and are obliged to renew their mortgages at rates of interest which would require an excessive proportion of their income. For borrowers with the same problem but with no substantial equity, the government will provide grants up to $3,000. The program will apply to mortgages renewed between September 1, 1981, and November 12, 1982. It will only be for home owners who are required to pay more than 30 per cent of their gross family income. It is really a scheme for home owners to borrow against equity to pare down their payments and to pay off the amount at a later date.
Housing
This grant and loan guarantee program will assist a total of
50,000	home owners out of nearly a million who will renew their home mortgages during the time limit imposed by the government. In fact, 37,500 of the 50,000 assisted will receive temporary help, but only 12,500 will receive real financial assistance.
Decent affordable accommodation is a basic right which all Canadians feel they should have. Housing is one of the most necessary of consumer goods. Buying a home is probably the largest single investment made by any family. Houses are purchased for investment or for security reasons. Every single Canadian has a direct interest in housing. People rent, own, construct or maintain a home, sometimes all of those things. Residential construction is a major industry and a significant segment of the economy.
It has been said that as the construction industry goes, so goes the economy. We are all aware of the sad situation with respect to the economy at the present time. When housing starts decline, renters and owners are not the only ones affected. A decline in housing starts has a snowball effect on many segments of the economy. The pressure on low-income people comes about by available housing becoming more costly. Reduced mobility of the work force is another very serious situation. This is caused by the unemployment connected with trades associated with construction, such as bricklayers, cabinet makers, plumbers and so on.
What about those selling or manufacturing bricks, insulation, carpets and on and on? Many bankruptcies have occurred in these particular industries. Some are just hanging on more or less by their teeth hoping that things will improve.
A depressed market results in less money in circulation. Cutbacks will, of course, have long-term effects. We are all aware how long it takes to build houses. You cannot have the economy change overnight and just say "presto" and have houses appear.
I can speak with some experience because I have been a real estate broker for a great number of years. I am not active at the present time, naturally, but I have a small firm that is operated by my sons. I checked with one of them today to find out how the little village of Burks Falls is affected by the serious situation in 1981. My son told me that by working his butt off in 1981 he managed to increase the business. I say more power to him. But in a great many cases housing sales have declined considerably. As a result, real estate brokers have been feeling the pinch too. That situation occurs not only in small places in Canada but even in the metropolitan areas with booming populations.
My hon. friend from Mississauga says the real estate market there has been very depressed. Mississauga was the fastest growing area in Canada. I do not know whether it has that same distinction now but its real estate market has been affected.
Being able to afford a home is very important. A great many people across Canada, both young and the not so young, all

February 9. 1982
Housing
hope some day to be able to purchase a home. However, because of high interest rates the affordability of housing has become a major problem.
As far as availability of housing is concerned, Canada needs just over 220,000 new housing units each year. In 1980, only
159,000	were built. In 1981, only 178,000 units were built. For 1982, the latest forecast predicts that only 180,000 units will be built. This will result in a shortage of 143,000 units over a three-year period.
High interest rates have resulted in a dramatic decline in the construction of new apartement units. For a landlord in Ontario to break even on the financing of a new building at today's interest rates, he would have to charge $800 per month for a one-bedroom apartment. Because this rate is more than double current rental rates, construction of buildings has all but ceased. The vacancy rate, or the number of housing units available to Canadians, has dropped dramatically all across the country. People just cannot find a place to live and cannot afford those that are available. The situation is getting worse and people are getting desperate.
In the third quarter of 1981, the price of an average home in Canada was $78,000. Assuming a 10 per cent down payment, $1,000 in property taxes and using the rule of thumb that total payments for principal, interest and taxes should not exceed 30 per cent of the gross family income, a family income of $44,500 is now needed to afford an average-priced home in Canada. House prices in the major cities, such as Toronto, Calgary and Vancouver, are higher. I understand that Vancouver has the distinction of having the highest priced housing in the country.
In 1978, mortgage rates were in the vicinity of 10.25 per cent. As most of us are aware, the rate now is in the vicinity of 18 per cent. The cost of an average home in 1978 was $55,000. The increase in the price of a home, coupled with higher interest rates, means a 129 per cent increase has occurred in the cost of servicing a mortgage on a new home. Approximately 1,200,000 Canadian families are facing renewal of their mortgages over the next two years. Those people renewing a 10 per cent mortgage at 18 per cent will see their monthly payment rise by 41 per cent. Some 40,000 Canadians are expected to lose their homes as a result.
Last fall the minister, as most of my colleagues will remember, asked members to write to him to give him specific cases of those people who would be losing their homes because of mortgages coming up for renewal during that very high interest rate period. I believe I wrote ten letters outlining ten cases to the minister. Some people came to my office almost crying. People were telling me that their payments in the $300 to $350 bracket would rise to the $700 bracket if they renewed their mortgages. Certain people told me that the mortgage companies had issued ultimatums to them saying they would not renew mortgages. I made it my business to contact either the head or the regional offices of the mortgage companies. In some cases, the mortgage companies stated that the individual mortgagor was slow in paying or was getting behind and the company was not interested in that kind of a hassle. Because of
insufficient annual income, mortgage companies knew that those who were having a difficult time paying their present mortgages would find it absolutely impossible to pay a rate half as much again. This put many of them in a very serious situation and they had to walk away from their homes.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the great budget of November 12, the help the poor and soak the rich budget, certainly has not done much for housing. There is virtually no relief for the housing market. The net effect may be that housing starts will plummet even further. The budget offers builders some assistance in the construction of apartments, but the interest-free loans of up to $7,500 per unit will only have a slight impact on the $800 per month break-even point faced by most builders.
I am also aware, Mr. Speaker, that only 15,000 units are going to be built under this plan. They are in certain areas where, in all fairness, the need is great but where the economy is probably the most buoyant. I do not think the small rural areas qualify. Toronto, maybe Hamilton, Calgary and Vancouver will. I am well aware they are just crying for apartments and houses, but that is where the money will be allocated. However, if we were to contact CMHC in Parry Sound-Muskoka or some other rural areas, I think we would find a line-up and nothing would be available.
We are all aware of the cancellation of MURB which was responsible for the construction of about 25,000 units last year,
10,000	more than the government expects from its new program. Of the $150 million available through this bill, $112 million will go to those 15,000 units, which leaves $38 million for all the other programs. And I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that is going to be spread pretty thin across the country.
The government is also reducing its commitment to subsidize social housing in 1982 from 30,000 to 25,000 units. These two policy decisions will result in a total reduction of 15,000 units. Only this blundering government would consider reducing incentives for the construction of rental housing in a period of severe rental housing shortage. Throughout the summer and fall the government promised to bring in some measure of relief for home owners in dire straits. However, the relief in the budget is little more than a program which allows people to keep their homes by going further and further into debt. In February, 1980, the Liberal government promised to make home ownership easier so that more Canadians could choose between renting and owning. Is this the way they keep their promise?
The Progressive Conservative Party believes an urgent need exists to provide relief to home owners in the form of mortgage interest and property tax credits. For a person renewing a $40,000 mortgage at 18 per cent, the tax credits would have lowered the effective interest rate to 14% per cent for the 1981 tax year, and to 13 'h per cent for the 1982 tax year.
Another reservoir of funds has dried up or may dry up, Mr. Speaker, because of this ridiculous budget and its regulations regarding life insurance. I suppose I could be accused of having a conflict of interest because I have had a licence to sell
February 9, 1982

life insurance since 1938, despite the fact that I am not doing so at this time. However, I am very familiar with the situation. Life insurance companies provide untold millions for home mortgages and for business.
I will admit, Mr. Speaker, that when I contacted the insurance company I was agent for and said that Mr. and Mrs. John Smith would like to have a mortgage in Burks Falls or Huntsville or wherever, I was very annoyed to be told that it just was not feasible for them to service a mortgage in that area; they would rather look out of the window of their skyscraper and say "We can loan all the money we want to right here and keep an eye on it". Mind you, that has changed down through the years and they now provide mortgage money for rural areas, but 1 can tell you that 25 or 30 years ago it was pretty difficult to get a life insurance or mortgage company to go into a small town. Of course, CMHC came along and did a good job. And then they did not do so good a job, so hold your applause.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member will accept a question at the termination of his remarks?

Yes, 1 will, Mr. Speaker. Now, the CMHC in its wisdom, when no other funds were available, made direct loans to individual home owners in villages and rural areas. Then, of course, some bureaucrat came along with the brilliant idea that these villages would no longer qualify unless they put in sewers. A good many of the small municipalities could not do that, and there was a period where finally someone got to the minister and the bureaucrats who made the decision, and it was changed so that they were able to get these direct loans.
1 want to emphasize again, Mr. Speaker, that I hope the minister responsible and other members on that side of the House will talk to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), quietly but in a persuasive manner, and tell him that he should forget all about the few paltry millions from the life insurance proceeds because it will not be worth sending out the bureaucrats and collectors to try to get the money. There are other more simple ways, and surely to God they will have enough brains to do it.
Those of us sitting here make a reasonable income. In fact, in the eyes of some it is an unreasonable income. Now, all you have to do is have those with an income of $50,000 or more pay 10 per cent more in taxes. We might squeal like stuck pigs, but that, in my view, is fairer than trying to squeeze it out of those in the very low income bracket.
Let me say that we on this side of the House are certainly in support of the bill. We are aware that in all probability the minister is more than aware of the serious situation. The minister had considerable experience before he was demoted. I hope he is listening to this because he, along with myself, served for many years in the highest form of government, that is municipal government; now we are in the lowest form of government! The minister, as the head of a very prosperous city, as a member of the great metro council, and also, I am quite sure, as a member of AMO, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, and other municipal organizations, should
Housing
know just how serious the situation is with respect to housing. I feel, and I hope I am right, that we do have more or less of a friend in court, as the minister knows the problems for small centres as well as big centres.
I want to mention one other problem which the hon. member who spoke previously mentioned, and I wish to commend him for it, and that is the problems of native people and those in rural areas concerning housing. I believe the minister did intimate that there will be another bill or something coming through which will particularly relate to rural and native housing. I say amen to that. I am also hoping that the RRAP, the Rural Rehabilitation Assistance Program, will be continued because that provides improved housing for areas in which there is no great boom of new housing. That is certainly important. Of course, some of that money is available in grant form to those who qualify on the means test.
We are all aware of the palace revolt. In this great metropolitan daily newspaper, I see the headline "Grits in Palace Revolt".
The Toronto Sun.
The Toronto Sun.
The bible of Toryism.
I do not know about that entirely, either; but it certainly keeps the Liberal government on its toes and may it continue to do so.
Hear, hear!

We are well aware of the palace revolt. I believe ten Members of Parliament were greatly concerned and I guess for very good reason, because they had been getting the message when they went to their respective ridings. Two of them were cabinet ministers. They were worried enough to write a letter to the king-emperor himself, voicing their disapproval in no uncertain terms, which took considerable courage.
Despite the fact that some people say the two cabinet ministers should resign because of this, I say that they should stay in cabinet and keep putting the heat on the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I know very well that it is not restricted to ten hon. members. The hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) was at home for five weeks, I assume; perhaps he was holidaying for part of the time, but I bet he got the message. Probably the only people who had a reasonably enjoyable and quiet holiday were the Members of Parliament in the opposition, because I do not know how any Liberal Member of Parliament could go out in public without being confronted by people concerned about the terrible budget, or MacEachenitis, or whatever one calls it.
A good many of our members can remember a task force on housing about a decade ago. I am now speaking about senior members of Parliament. I know I was not here at the time, and

February 9, 1982
Housing
in looking around this august chamber today, I do not see too many in the House who were here at that time. There are two hon. members on our side who were probably here. This task force on housing was instituted and headed by the hon. Paul Hellyer, who was responsible for housing at the time, I believe. Paul Hellyer came out with an outstanding report and presented it to the cabinet. 1 believe it recommended that one million homes be built over the following five years. The Prime Minister took it, and I guess he put it up on the shelf and let it gather dust. Mr. Hellyer was so disenchanted that he resigned from the cabinet; he later resigned from the Liberal government when he saw the light and came over to this side of the House. When he was defeated, the House of Commons certainly lost an outstanding parliamentarian.
As I mentioned before, we are still in a continually high interest rate period although interest rates have come down from the highest level reached back in September of 1981, I believe, when mortgage rates reached the astronomical figure of 21.4 per cent. I know that at that particular time businessmen were paying 24 per cent and 25 per cent for loans at their banks. As a result of that, many of them ended up by going bankrupt, and some are still simply hanging on. We are still in the 18 per cent bracket when it comes to renewing mortgages, and this is certainly a serious situation.
In 1965, the average new home cost about $17,000, and older homes were even less. In 1981, the average home cost $74,000 and, of course, much more in some cities. I am also aware that the average wage in 1965 was about $5,000 and that the interest rate was pretty well around the 7 per cent bracket. I guess we all wish that we could come back to the 7 per cent bracket, but not necessarily to the $5,000 average wage.
The average income in Canada today is about $18,000, with mortgage rates in the 17 per cent and upward range. However, estimates now state that in certain areas the average house will cost $100,000 to build, which is far beyond the capability of well over 90 per cent of the people of Canada.
Let us not forget that last fall a great many irate people appeared on Parliament Hill whose mortgages were coming due on their homes. I can tell hon. members that they comprised a very unhappy group. They wanted to talk to people. I believe they did talk to a group, and they spoke to the minister in one of the committee rooms in the West Block. I happen to be one of those who went out on the Hill and was able to speak to a good many of these home owners. I asked them, "Well, how did you vote in the last election?" Needless to say, a considerable number of them said that they voted Liberal, but they would never vote that way again. I said, "Well, it serves you damn well right." 1 said, "1 should not say that. 1 certainly feel sympathy for you, but that is the message I want to try to get across to you."
Stan, Stan!

That is true. That is just telling it like it is. It was amazing to hear the stories of these people, who were very worried. One particular man was getting on in years, and by
that I mean he was not very young. I said, "Have you got a mortgage?" He said, "No but I am here to protest because my daughter and her husband have a mortgage and it looks as though they will lose their home." He was a resident of Ottawa. I am quite sure that a good many of the people who appeared on Parliament Hill finally had to decide that there was nothing else to do but to take the keys and hand them back to the mortgagees, and then walk away to look for some sort of rental accommodation within their budgets.
We are all well aware of the tragedy which occurred two or three weeks ago in the little village of Spanish, Ontario, up in the Sudbury area. Nine people died in a fire there, including a family of seven. As most hon. members have read, this particular family was purchasing a home in Spanish. In fact, I have seen a picture of it, and it was a modern bungalow. Because of the drastic increase in the family's mortgage payment as a result of high interest rates, they finally decided that there was just no way they could swing it and keep it. They just walked away from that home and moved into an apartment in a converted school. As a result of moving there, they all burned to death.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: How do you feel about that, Paul?

A case like this could happen time and time again. We know that many people here in Canada are living in very poor accommodation, accommodation which is unquestionably unsafe under fire standards and maybe under health standards as well. Something must be done.
The minister must get the message across to the rest of his government that housing is important. We must do something concrete so that it will help a great many more people than it seems this bill will help. In the past, I heard one of the hon. members mention that literally billions of dollars have flown from Canada to the United States because the economic climate is more attractive there. Interest rates are higher. When the interest rates again go up here, some of this money will return. I am aware of this and I am sure the minister must be as well. Many successful developers who are developing and have developed land, built homes and apartments, have reached the point where the economic climate is not satisfactory in Canada, so they have gone to the United States where they are welcomed with open arms. That is a fine state of affairs when we are literally crying for housing here.
The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the federal government are partly to blame, but not entirely. As 1 mentioned in the House, the other levels of government are also to blame. There is the red tape of the municipal governments, the damn planners, zoners, and all the rest who hold up the development of buildings. Consequently the developers have said "That's it".
Each time there is a delay, it adds to the cost of the land. The developers borrow money on a short-term basis. When interest was at 12 per cent, money was borrowed for short periods in order that they could get the plans ready and the
February 9. 1982

lots subdivided. By the time they were ready to build, they were paying 16 and 17 per cent. This is because they had been held up by the bureaucracy.
Some municipalities in the United States have come up with a brilliant idea which I wish our municipal and provincial governments would adopt. They presented their idea to the planners and citizens' groups. If an apartment or housing development is going to be built in a certain area, there are always many citizens who do not want the additional traffic, housing and schools, and they immediately start petitions. This causes delay, delay, delay and raises the cost of housing. It also cuts down on the amount of housing available.
In certain areas of the United States they have decided to cut down on the long delays. The planners, zoners, and municipal groups which have to approve these matters are being told that the procedure will be done in reverse. Rather than plans sitting on their desk for months or even years, they are given 90 days in which they had better come up with a damned good reason why the project should be delayed or it will go through automatically. If we followed that procedure here, it would help the housing industry and would probably result in cheaper housing.
I hope the minister will accept some of these suggestions presented by members on all sides of the House. He is aware that much needs to be done. We on this side have presented various suggestions with regard to housing. As we stated, mortgage interest deductibility and municipal tax deductibility are both suggestions that should be considered. I bet that a great many of the thousands of people who voted Liberal in February, 1980, wished they had the opportunity to vote again today. They would welcome that program with open arms.
Having been a municipal mayor for a number of years, I am sure the minister will agree that having to pay tax on tax is unfair. Why should people who pay municipal taxes to Scarborough or to the village of Burks Falls not be able to deduct that amount from their income tax up to a certain level?
When I was a vice-president of the Ontario Mayors and Reeves Association, I made that suggestion. It received the endorsement of 90 per cent of those who were present, but did not get very far when it came to Ottawa, where it was just thrown in the ashcan. It is one area where a home owner would get a break. This has been done in the United States for years. We have adopted some of their other tax measures, such as capital gains.
This brings me to another can of worms, the capital gains tax and the way it is being tightened up. According to the Minister of Finance, all businessmen have more or less been tarred as crooks. That is it in a nutshell. In a holier-than-thou attitude on November 12, the minister said that he would tighten all loopholes for businessmen and women, yet those "loopholes" were legitimate business expenses.
Absolutely.

They were brought in by the government in the first place, having been dreamed up by the bureaucrats. I
Housing
spoke to the former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), about this. He said that those same bloody bureaucrats brought those suggestions to him, but he told them where to put them. Why did the present Minister of Finance not do the same?
Something else that affects the economy and housing is the capital cost allowance, which has been reduced. The minister in his wisdom says it will make no difference. I can tell him that it will make a considerable difference to those who were going to expand their operations and purchase additional equipment. They are no longer going to do that.
There were 17 items on which the minister recanted on December 18. Many of us are still worried about the effect that some of the items he listed will have. Some are just a delay. Others may be good and he may follow through with them. Before the budget is finally passed, I hope the minister will take seriously the suggestions with which he has been bombarded. 1 also hope that this housing bill will provide more money than originally intended.

The province of British Columbia is well-off and can look after its own housing problems; it does not need to come to the federal government for assistance. This government should stick to the areas in which it performs well and not go into areas of provincial jurisdiction-
