speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question was, who is representing the position of the Conservative Party, the last speaker or the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn)?

Mr. Speaker, I presume that the minister will be in his seat this evening. The hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) will be speaking later this evening and I suggest that he direct his question to him.
As far as Vancouver, British Columbia, is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I represent a rural area, not one of the great wealthy areas like a borough of metropolitan Toronto or even wealthy British Columbia, although there are poverty pockets even there. Therefore, I feel that the government certainly has a job to do to assist the housing industry. Regardless, that is the message I will deliver and continue to deliver.

Madam Speaker, I should like to comment on this bill, which affects a major sector of the economy in Canada and particularly in Quebec, namely, housing. Two years ago, in a situation similar to the one we have today, our friends opposite were objecting to a program we had brought in, which today, as the minister is aware, would provide $150 per month. The bill was voted down with the help of the New Democratic Party, which is now complaining that nothing has been done for two years. Looking back, Canadians must realize that the solution we proposed 24
months ago was the right one, considering the situation prevailing today. What has happened since? Not much, except for an election and a government that is categorically opposed to helping home owners and is letting a major industry, namely, residential construction, go into bankruptcy.
Yesterday, the minister asked us to pass the bill quickly. I can see why he would rather not have a long debate in the House, and if I were in his shoes, I would feel very uncomfortable. However, I believe some of the members of this House will remind the minister, and he deserves to be reminded, that a bill that is supposed to help only 10 per cent of those who need help is entirely unsatisfactory and incomplete. When everyone keeps repeating that 40,000 Canadians stand to lose their homes, the minister comes up with a proposal that is going to help one out of ten, and only under certain conditions.
Since the session resumed, I have been trying to make my colleagues wake up to various facts such as the present state of the economy, a budget that is unacceptable, the hundreds of representations coming from all parts of the country and the present high rate of unemployment. Today, we are concerned with housing. I remember, Mr. Speaker, I probably forgot to tell the House about this. In August, 1981, when I was returned to Parliament after a byelection, one of the three main points I stressed in my campaign was the lack of a policy on interest rates, which was causing so much suffering and concern and had caused thousands of people to lose their homes-I shall be giving some figures later on, not my own, but provided by a highly respected organization. It was clear that people were very unhappy about the fact that nothing was being done and wanted action, so I promised the people of the riding of Joliette that I would go and remind the minister that he had a responsibility here, and would ask him to have a little more guts and use his influence to persuade the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), who refuses to listen or talk to them. I believe our repeated attacks were successful in waking up ten of our colleagues who actually went so far as to sign a piece of paper. Incredible! Mr. Speaker, either this is some kind of joke, and the public will be their judge, or these people are in earnest. If they are, it means that by writing to the Prime Minister and publishing their letter, they are actually admitting they are unable to speak to the Prime Minister directly, and this group includes two ministers.
Or else it is part of a plan, considering the results of the recent federal-provincial conference, where the government lost the confidence of the ten provincial premiers, and considering the fierce opposition from all parts of the country, with organizations actually telling the government that it is leading the country straight into bankruptcy. The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) realizes that he can no longer keep his Minister of Finance or in any case maintain his economic philosophy which has been a colossal failure-and it wasn't me that said it at the federal-provincial conference! In the circumstances, the Right Hon. Prime Minister is clever enough not to
February 9, 1982

want to give the credit to all his opponents. The Minister of Finance has to be allowed to backtrack, and with this plan * involving two ministers and eight other members, the Right Hon. Prime Minister would subsequently be able to say that he backtracked because of internal pressures. If that were true, not ten but at least 50 members would have signed the letter.
I wonder whether the members for Frontenac (Mr. Cor-riveau) and Duvernay (Mr. Demers), whom I saw a while ago, and the member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) would have signed the letter as well. And today, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mrs. Begin) had even harsher words than usual in front of the television cameras, and during oral question period, we had this absurd situation where the Right Hon. Prime Minister felt he had to challenege his caucus and his members. He looked them in the eye and asked them: It isn't true you don't support me, is it? And the Minister of National Health and Welfare even applauded. Quite a show. Unfortunately, this is the kind of attitude I have often seen around here. I was reading in yesterday's Hansard the speech made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette) who, after signing the letter in which they asked for emergency measures in the housing sector, because they realized that the country was losing 50,000 units, asked us to push this bill through at top speed. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but I think there are members of the official opposition who have some comments they want to make to the minister, and I have felt for quite some time that the minister must feel very dissatisfied about his failure to convince the Minister of Finance that more should be done than what he is giving us today. This bill is deplorable, and it fails to meet any of the needs of Canadians today.
The present government seems to forget that to turn the economy around, it has to do more than increase its expenditures by 22 per cent and put hundreds of thousands of people out of work as a result of the energy agreement, which is generating billions for the federal treasury. The government should have redistributed this revenue fairly and used the money to turn around the most productive sectors of our economy, including the construction industry. Mr. Speaker, the House will agree that the situation has been very tough in this sector during the last two years. A sector that involves 33 per cent of the labour force has been ignored. Once more, the minister is going to ask us to trust him, to support his policies and to help pass this entirely inadequate measure. If we consider the construction industry's significance as a producer of economic spin-offs and as an industry that generates 30 per cent of the jobs in this country, it is really hard to believe that a federal subsidy affecting 15,000 housing units in Canada, including between 1,000 and 1,500 in Quebec, is going to turn around construction, when we actually need 200,000 units. In Quebec alone, at least 35,000 units are needed each year.
Housing
Because there is a shortage of new housing, the construction industry is in a slump, there is a shortage of accommodation and rents are inflated.
I also deplore the lack of any concrete measures to promote the recovery of the building industry. I greatly deplore the fact that the government has failed to implement our proposal to set a preferential interest rate for mortgages, thus enabling thousands of home owners to keep their homes and thousands of other Canadians to realize their legitimate dream of becoming home owners. Nothing has been done in this regard, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that socially, to become a home owner is something good and positive for an individual. He becomes more committed to his own municipality, to his province and to his country. Nothing in this legislation confirms that the government pursues that objective.
Of course, 12,000 Canadian taxpayers out of approximately
900.000	who will face renewal of their mortgages in 1982 will receive assistance. No one can deny that enabling renters to become home owners not only has very positive social and human consequences but also enriches the community and contributes to the general welfare. I would also like to point out that the budget of the Conservative government included a proposal which would have helped home owners. That proposal involved a $150 monthly credit, as I said earlier. That type of housing credit would have prevented the social tragedy that we experienced last year and are still experiencing. It is useless to blame the United States and international economic conditions because nothing prevents a government with some sense of morality and social responsibility to implement a special program of preferential interest rates, which would at the same time be a good way to boost the building industry.
I am thinking, Mr. Speaker, about some of the figures mentioned yesterday in the House when my hon. friend for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) said the following:
We know that the proposals contained in this bill will affect only about 12,000 households in Canada out of approximately 900,000 which will be renewing. It barely addresses the problem, and those who are in "dire straits"-a term used by the Prime Minister in addressing what the government intended to do; he suggested it would help those in dire straits-can look forward to a one-time payment. Yet we are told that mortgage interest rates are on the way back up again after falling from the high of 21.4 per cent of last September. We are told they are on their way back up again and will again reach 20 per cent this year.
It is obvious that the legislation now before uS does not provide this assurance and encouragement to those who want to become home owners. To meet the needs of the Canadian people, an average of 220,000 housing starts a year would be needed between 1981 and 1986. In 1981, there were only
178.000	housing starts while 222,000 would have been necessary to meet our needs.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to quote a few figures, those of the Quebec Homebuilders Association. In 1976, there were 68,748 housing starts; in 1977, 57,580; in 1978, 43,671; in 1979, 41,730; in 1980, 29,186; in 1981, 29,500, and 26,000 are expected in 1982. Mr. Speaker, this shows how important it is

February 9, 1982
Housing
to deal with this matter today, and I think it would be interesting for the minister to realize the negative impact of such a lack of measures and how costly it is for Canadians. For example, I have here a report of the eastern township branch of the same organization, from which I would like to quote the following excerpt:
We would like to point out to you that every thousand dwellings that remain unbuilt results in a dead and irremediable loss of $84 million for the gross national product as well as a loss of 680 direct jobs and 580 indirect jobs, not to mention the 950 jobs lost through the multiplying effects.
A quick calculation-and it is important that the minister know this and realize exactly what this government is responsible for in the end-a quick calculation reveals that 44,000 units were not built in 1981, keeping in mind the needs of Canada, and that it entails the loss of 30,000 direct jobs, a loss of 25,520 jobs and a total loss of 41,800 jobs if we take the multiplier effect into consideration. That amounts to a gross national product loss of $3,696 billion. That is the result of a lack of policy which happens to be of great significance to Canadians who need it.
Mr. Speaker, I am thinking about those figures and the prevailing situation across Canada, about those hon. members who dared speak their mind ever so gently and very politely castigate the Minister of Finance and his colleague responsible for housing for failing to do the bare minimum. 1 hope there are more than ten on the other side. When I look at the current situation in my province alone-I say that because a lot of members from my province sit across the aisle-I have the impression that there must be at least five times as many who feel the same way. They would not run the risk of being called dirty names as some of them were by the Societe Saint-Jean-Baptiste not so long ago. As Quebecers and Canadians, I suggest we have responsibilities and duties in the House.
I told the people of my riding of Joliette that I would urge this government to take measures which meet their needs and which flow from moral and social responsibilities. That is what I am doing today. I strongly condemn this minister and this government for failing to propose adequate measures. One member from Quebec spoke last night, and I hope there will be others. 1 hope that the ten members who signed that letter will stand up and rake the minister over the coals, as I am doing, because he failed to come up with a measure to meet the minimum requirements of thousands of Canadians. Then again, maybe the whole thing was a big joke to enable the Prime Minister to discredit members of the opposition who for too long have been doing their job and discharging their daily responsibilities in seeking improved benefits for people who are suffering. In the short term, there may not be 25 solutions, there are no miracle solutions, true enough, but we have to make a choice. There are certain classes of people who cannot be left to fend for themselves.
Today I will not mention the thousands of home owners who, in addition to interest rates, have to cope with a problem created by an unacceptable product, urea formaldehyde foam insulation, which the government approved but for which it will not take any responsibility. There are enough Canadians who are suffering as I speak. There are enough Canadians whose first ambition is to become home owners. Thousands of Canadians are worried and wondering whether they will be able to keep their own home. God knows how hard they worked and did everything they could to keep their home!
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that there is no need debating in the house day after day and asking this government to come to its senses. Would it be that the Prime Minister has lost all contact with reality? Is the Minister of Finance persevering in his lunacy to the point where ten hon. members and, I hope, more of them, will press him further?
How can a government imagine that it still deserves the public's confidence when it leaves so many problems unsolved? How can the minister responsible for housing still sleep soundly tonight, feeling that he is answering the needs of Canadians? 1 do not doubt the minister's intention to try to obtain more from the Minister of Finance, but if indeed he has tried, I must tell him now that he has failed miserably. We have known other ministers who had needs and who had made known the respective needs of their departments, and who have failed in their efforts to communicate with this Minister of Finance who will not hear anything nor accept the fact that his current policy, in line with his predecessors' policies, is a complete failure. On behalf of thousands of Canadians, and Quebecers too, I can say to the housing minister that there are in Canada people who have problems-these figures are selfexplanatory-
They are Canadians too!

Yes, they are Canadians too. Perhaps the member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) could tell me what else is new. I was referring to Quebecers because I am from Quebec, and other members are going to talk about Ontario or Alberta. Mr. Speaker, whatever I say, they are going to be offended. I want to ask the Minister of Housing to make a statement and to give us something better than this inadequate legislation. I am sure, and I cannot say it often enough, that if they have been forced to take a position, there must be more than ten members who think this way. It just is not possible that only the opposition takes this view. I believe the members opposite also have a responsibility, and I feel that we must, that it is our duty, to demand that they do more and do it better. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, it was generally felt last week, no longer have the confidence of the provincial premiers. That is obvious. I wonder how long the Prime Minister is going to persist in his stubborn attitude, while Canada's problems get worse and worse. People say he is going to retire. He may not give a damn, but he has no right to make Canadians suffer the
February 9, 1982

way he is doing now through his own stubbornness and the attitude taken by his Minister of Finance. I want to tell the minister responsible for housing, who needs our support, that we are with him all the way, but not unless he brings in measures that do more than this non-legislation being served up in the House today. Canadians need more than that, and thousands of Canadians are demanding action by the government. The Canadian economy needs to be stimulated, and this can be done by stimulating the construction industry. Thousands of people would get their jobs back. That is why 1 am making these demands today, and I will continue to do so as long as the government fails to respond satisfactorily to the needs of our constituents across Canada, including those in my own province.
Mr. Speaker, I shall give other members a chance to express their views and make their comments. I hope that there will soon be a measure to deal with interest rates, that there will be programs, and although the program proposals may differ, we know perfectly well that there are not 15 different ways of lowering interest rates in order to turn around the construction industry and give Canadians a chance to have their own homes. Special interest rates are necessary, whatever the program or arrangement, but they should not be restricted to
15,000	units, as the minister said today. Shelter should be a right and it should be available. If this is part of our social policies, it should also be part of the policy of the minister responsible for housing. It should also be part of the philosophy of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, who was talking about a just society only 15 years ago.
Mr. Speaker, we have come a long way since then and our society seems to be getting less and less just. 1 think many Canadians are realizing that too many promises have never been kept. Today, I once more want to ask this government to provide just and equitable measures that will help thousands of Canadians make a happier life for themselves.

Mr. Speaker, a few minutes earlier the minister for housing, who is no better at asking questions than he is at answering them, made some comments with respect to certain comments of mine at an earlier point. Clearly the minister must understand that the provincial governments which are involved in housing in terms of land, land assembly and land servicing-by and large are able to direct the planning of their provinces adequately to make sure that houses can be built, and where we have land costs that are totally outrageous, as we have in British Columbia, or certainly had, that a lot of those problems are stemming from areas of provincial responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, the major national responsibility which the minister refuses to accept is his government's totally inept handling of the interest rate concerns in this country and particularly how those interest rate concerns affect the housing industry. That total ineptness was no more pronounced than could be pronounced in the budget of November 12.
Housing
In the past months or year or year and a half, we have seen the total destruction of the capital markets of the country. It is not very long ago that a person borrowed money on a mortgage for 25 years. That slipped to ten years, then to five years, and now, even in accordance with the admission of the minister, to six months. You know, we almost have the interest rates for the long-term financing of Canadian housing today determined every Thursday on the auction of 90-day treasury bills.
Mr. Speaker, this condition in the long-term financial markets of the country lies totally at the doorstep of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the colleague of this minister who now apologetically brings before the House a makeshift, shabby piece of legislation, patchwork of the worst order, to try to solve, in a patchwork type fashion-to try to solve but not even begin to solve, some of the problems that the financial policies of his government have created.
Let me deal briefly, Sir, with the budget and how it destroyed the long-term markets even further than they were already destroyed. The minister will know that one of the major sources of medium and long-term money in this country, perhaps the greatest source, has been the insurance industry. What does this budget do? It attacks the insurance industry, it attacks annuities, it attacks all types of long-term savings, by trying to create a deemed income concept. The insurance industry declared before public hearings, both here in Ottawa and in London and in Kitchener, that that industry will lose at least $1.75 billion of long-term capital for long-term investment in the economy of this country for housing, if you want to put it that way, in this year alone by the action in this budget.
What does the budget do? It attacks registered retirement savings plans by discouraging people from borrowing on a short-term basis to purchase them. It discourages long-term savings and wipes out the IAAC program. It makes deferred annuities unpalatable and attacks long-term life insurance. If the government was looking to do damage to people who wanted mortgages for decent periods of time, it could not have done it better. Where was the minister when that matter arose? Has the minister written a letter, as did his cabinet colleague who is sitting beside him now, to the Minister of Finance and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) respecting housing concerns?
What have we heard from the government in connection with long-term capital? John Acheson, president of Dominion Life, said that the effects of the budget with its deemed income provisons will further damage what savings are left in the insurance industry by forcing that industry to keep more and more of its money in short-term investments, because it will be obligated to look after the distribution of income every three years to policyholders and annuitants to pay their income taxes.
The effects of the budget with respect to registered retirement savings plans, IAACs, deferred annuities and life insurance, destroy one of our great sources of long-term capital and pins us even further to the day by day market situation where

February 9, 1982
Housing
people cannot find money for a ten-year, 20-year or 25-year commitment; they will only obtain 90 day commitments.
Gerald Voisin of Kitchener spoke to us during our hearings in that city. He said that builders today were playing Russian roulette. If brave enough they start projects, but in order to do so they are required to do an analysis of the cash flow. He asked how builders could calculate their interest rates. Are they to take 18 per cent out of the sky and say that that will be the interest rate? They cannot obtain commitments on projects which will be open for business, for example, in September. Builders will not be able to fix interest rates on their projects until September, and then they would only be fixed for one year. One must be nuts or playing Russian roulette to commence a building operation in the private market with the present monetary system. What is the minister's attitude toward apartment construction? What about these $7,500 loans? What about the balance of the cash? There is no fixed interest on the balance of the cash. There is no place where a builder can obtain ten-year or 20-year mortgage money to determine his carrying costs, fix his project and package it. Unless there is some stability in the marketplace, $7,500 interest-free loans, about which I will speak later, are absolutely useless.
The government attempts to say that it is doing something for housing in this patchwork bill, but it does not even begin to look at the problems which now exist. It clearly throws out the MURB program. Perhaps there was good reason for doing that, perhaps there were some abuses of the program; there were certainly some problems. But it does not get down to the brass tacks of encouraging investors into the marketplace. The attitude of government in its $7,500 loans for apartment construction indicates that it believes big government knows best where to put the building and what are the housing requirements.
For a moment I should like to talk about the interest rate problem. All hon. members know that to carry a $15,000 mortgage at 10 per cent costs approximately $447 per month. At 20 per cent, it is nearly doubled to $807 per month. There are massive changes in what people can afford to carry. A person who borrowed at 10.5 per cent in 1978 is now looking down the pipe at 19.5 per cent or 9 per cent more, but his or her income has not risen proportionately to carry the cost of the debt. This is one of the reasons for the problems with AHOP loans. People were sucked into buying houses on the basis that they thought they were receiving reasonably longterm financing from the government. They found out they were receiving only five-year financing and that their interest rates doubled. When they were committed up to the hilt to purchase properties, there was no way their incomes could conceivably increase to meet virtual double payments five years later. That is the essence of the situation.
Perhaps the problem is worse today than it was prior to the budget. When a person decides to purchase a house, he is looking at a six-month or one-year mortgage at 18.5 per cent or 19 per cent. What will he do in six months' time when his
mortgage comes due? Will interest rates this August be 20.5 per cent or 20.75 per cent, as they were last August?
Before coming into the House today I heard that American interest rates were up again and that the U.S. T bill rate auctioned today at 14.10 per cent. If the government follows the trend in American interest rates and does its usual thing, interest rates in Canada will rise once again and there will be the Thursday auction concept whereby the cost of financing property will vary almost weekly. How can a young couple, or anyone for that matter, make a long-term commitment to purchase a home with the idea that the Thursday cost might be different next Thursday or the following one? We cannot expect people to buy or commit themselves on that basis. Builders cannot work on that basis, prospective owners cannot buy on that basis. The bill does not address the problem.
The ministry issued a CMHC paper entitled, "CMHC 6-81 BP", to which I should like to refer. It indicated that over the next two years approximately 1.2 million households will be renewing their mortgages. It also set out the tables on those mortgages and indicated that most of those households will be able to do so, although adjustments will be painful. It indicated that for these households house payments will increase but that they will still be paying less than 30 per cent of income for mortgage debt. Also it went on to indicate that their equity will allow them to take steps to reduce their mortgages and that 30,000 to 40,000 households cannot even take steps to help themselves and retain their homes.
Presumably it was as a result of this report that the minister came up with the most half-baked expropriatory program ever conceived by any government. Mr. Speaker, when you and I purchased our homes we may have assumed mortgages and made payments on them. Every time we made payments we felt that the debt was reduced a little. Perhaps it was only $10 or $15 per month, but at least it was something. The government says that you use 30 per cent of your gross income toward housing payments. You use all of your blood and sweat to pay the payments, and if you have $44,000 worth of mortgages, like Fernando Brunetti at 2500 Harmond Court in Mississauga, you go into this kind of scheme advocated by the minister. But after a year, you do not owe $44,000, you owe $46,000. What kind of a disgraceful, immoral, indecent suggestion is that? That is the very suggestion contemplated in the guarantee provisions to the insurance and trust companies in this bill. You use 30 per cent of your gross income, your blood and sweat, and you pay and pay and pay, and at the end of the year you owe $2,000 more than you did at the beginning of the year. All of that is justified because you have equity in your property and you are borrowing against your equity. In other words, the Brunettis can live in their house. They cannot afford to do so, but the government says: just live there and owe more and more money. In other words, operate just like the Government of Canada. The government cannot pay its bills, so it borrows more. This bill creates an immoral and indecent suggestion.
February 9, 1982

It is true that the bill goes on to do something for those people who eventually get to the point where they have no equity. For those people, the minister says "I will be nice to your big bank or trust company. I will pay your big bank or trust company up to $3,000 so they will not throw you out until after November 12, 1982."
Here we have a problem that is going to suck people in to greater and greater debt. These are debts they cannot pay today because they do not have enough income to pay the payments today. But after November 12, 1982, they will owe, as in the case of the Brunetti family, $2,000 more than they already owe. They cannot pay the interest on $44,000 because of this interest rate policy of the government. I do not know how people can pay interest on $46,000. Until interest rates decline 6 per cent, the Brunettis do not get into a positive position of 30 per cent of their gross income for housing. Isn't that great? We have a situation where we know people cannot afford the interest on the $44,000 at the current demanded rate of the trust company, so we say: capitalize the interest. But we know that the effect of capitalizing interest will be to increase the debt by $2,000. We know in our heart of hearts that we only have to look in the financial pages to see what the money markets are like and we know that interest rates will not be down 6 per cent by November 12, 1982. We know, and the minister knows, that the Brunettis will be up the creek for $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Does the hon. member stand by his offer to accept a question at the end of his remarks?

I will be most delighted, Mr. Speaker.
I want to leave the question of this despicable system where people owe more after a year than they already now owe. This is a condition certified more or less by this bill. Indeed, the bill offers to guarantee that kind of arrangement.
I want to go to the next matter dealt with in the bill which is that of allowing the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to deal with premiums on its insurance fund.
I suppose I was quite refreshed yesterday when the minister spoke. He said that if his actuaries had looked at AHOP and how to ensure AHOP mortgages properly, they should have received a premium of 8 per cent of the amount of money involved on each AHOP mortgage.
We all know that if Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation had to charge a premium of 8 per cent as a mortgage insurance fee, there would not have been any AHOP in the first place. A discount of 8 per cent on a $44,000 mortgage is $3,200. That would have been the fee. If that had been the case, there would not have been any AHOP at all. That probably would have been good for Canada. This party was not really in favour of it. I am sure that my friends to the left were not all that hot to trot with AHOP either. AHOP was essentially a deferred mortgage payment program. The same type of philosophy that is behind this "borrow on your equity
Housing
program" contained in this bill is a philosophy developed by the officials in the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This minister says that that type of insurance, his actuaries tell him, would cost 8 per cent. That should tell the minister something. That should tell the minister that he has some pretty poor officials in his ministry and in the corporation. These were the people who thought out AHOP and who got the corporation into a financial mess in its mortgate insurance account and lost $600 million or $700 million. This is the group of people who now determine that the insurance fee should be 8 per cent for an AHOP mortgage. Yet this is the group that would go on and on with a program to add interest to debt and put people closer and closer to bankruptcy.
Surely the minister must see through the advice that he is getting. Surely the minister must, in that very analysis of his insurance fee, understand what has happened.
I made a suggestion yesterday in this House. I put a question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. MacLellan) who, I presume, has something to do with this particular field. I asked whether the parliamentary secretary could indicate whether the new provisions in this bill would enable the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to guarantee a fixed rate of interest for five years.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the House rose at six o'clock, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, immediately before the dinner adjournment I was commenting on a question I asked of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. I asked him if one of the reasons for the change in the insurance provisions of the act was to allow CMHC to guarantee a fixed rate of interest for five years on payment of an appropriate fee. I made that suggestion because that might be a worth-while thing for the corporation to do. I know the minister wants to ask me some questions with respect to where I or my party may stand, and I suggest that in the process he might answer that question.
Next, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with apartment shortages that exist throughout Canada. Clearly it is because of this government's program with respect to handling accommodation as an investment that we have gone from a situation where apartment landlords were prepared to give you a trip to

February 9, 1982
Housing
Florida or three months rent free along with all sorts of other advantages if you signed a lease, to one where we have now in Mississauga, according to a report I received today from the corporation, a vacancy rate of 0.3 per cent. That is a reduction from 0.8 per cent in the past year, and clearly all the indications in the minister's own report with respect to rental accommodation are that we are very rapidly getting to the point where there will be absolutely no rental accommodation in the country.
In making that statement. Sir, I ask you to look at our past history. From 1971 to 1973 we were constructing 106,000 apartment units a year, and we produced them because we allowed the owners to deduct the capital cost and associated carrying charges from their other income. We treated apartments the same as we would any ordinary investment income. Now I want to point out that anyone who has ever been involved in the building business, whether building apartments, office complexes, a group of stores or shopping centres, knows the project will not carry itself in the first, second or third years from rent alone. In that case the owner or developer has to have some method whereby he can write off new project losses against other income.
Now ever since 1971, when we changed the Income Tax Act around, the tax laws have prevented those who would invest in rental accommodation from treating it as a business. The consequences are that if you are collecting rent and that is your only business, it does not qualify under the small business provisions of the Income Tax Act. You cannot write off the cost of a car used to collect the rent, or other things associated with that project. If the rent you collect is insufficient to cover your martgage interest or capital costs associated with the building, you cannot deduct those costs from other income. It has to be confined to the rental from the building.
Now, Sir, those very conditions imposed by this government in its tax changes have led to the situation where investors look at residential rental units as a no-no, something you do not want to invest in. And the minister wonders why we have a shortage. Now, of all things, we have a situation where the government comes along and says to those who build rental accommodation: Well, here is $7,500 for free, build us a suite.
That is not the way to go about it. We do not need the bureaucracy of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, we do not need a series of grants and a series of proposals to understand that there will never be a situation where any government can ever provide enough grants or make enough payments to individuals to get them to do something which does not make business sense.
I therefore ask the minister, who is here tonight, will he please look at the whole problem? He should look at the situation we had prior to these changes to the Income Tax Act with the surplus of rental accommodation we had in those years and compare it with the deficit in rental accommodation we have today. He would then realize that it is not the builders, it is not the developers, it is not the rich landlords and it is not provincial rent controls which have caused the problems. The problem has been caused because the economics of the matter, which have been determined by tax laws, among many other things, have militated against apartment construction. The $7,500 grant for each of 15,000 units is a bag of nothing. It will not solve the problem of the shortage of rental accommodation in Canada this year. It will not even go partway there. The minister will know that from 1971 to 1972 we built an average of 106,000 apartment units a year. In 1981, we built 52,000 apartment units, of which 35,000 had to be government assisted, and only 17,000 were built by the private market on its own. The forecast in the minister's own briefing notes is that there will be precious little, if any, construction next year without some sort of government assi-tance. The fact is that if we were to change the tax laws and get back to realities, we would wind up with a private market which would satisfy our needs.
I want to leave that subject of apartment shortages for a moment. It is a horrendous problem. It means that shortly people will pay key money to have an apartment. People who cannot afford an apartment will have to live with mother. As mentioned by other hon. members, the costs of a one-bedroom unit today amount to $750 to $800 a month, if the true costs were calculated.
However, aside from the social problems which this situa-[DOT] tion creates, we will get nowhere with this business of continuing to make grants in an attempt to bribe builders to build something which is not worth building, because they will not ' receive the financial returns they would normally expect to receive.
Let us really deal with the real problem. The problem boils down to interest rates. As Your Honour knows, we as a party held hearings right across Canada in 14 cities. One hundred and sixty-eight witnesses came before us. Many of those witnesses were involved in builder organizations and real estate board organizations. They were people who were concerned about housing and people in the housing field. When we asked what kind of interest rate people could realistically afford to pay under the present economic climate, the answers came back to us that it would be somewhere between 12 per cent and 14 per cent. The Hamilton district building group said that over a 14 per cent interest rate, every increase by one per cent eliminates 25 per cent of the purchasers. The same applies, of course, to apartment rents, because it is obvious that no one will build an apartment building without getting a mortgage on it, and one must pass the mortgage interest on to the rent charged. Therefore, we are not making any distinction between owners and renters.
What we must have is a government which is prepared to come to grips with the fact that interest on housing loans must be at a fixed rate, one which the purchasers or renters can reasonably afford to pay on the basis of their incomes. Somewhere along the line, a government must divorce the housing cost of money from the commercial cost of money for ordinary business transactions. This is because, when one builds a building, it should last for 25, 35 or 50 years. Indeed, the amortization of a building was originally thought to be a
February 9, 1982

50-year proposition. One is building a long-term asset, and the debt should be paid off in around 25 to 30 years. The debt must be guaranteed for that period, and the interest rate on that debt must be guaranteed for much longer than six months. It must be guaranteed for a year, two years or three years, which is presently the duration of guarantees today. Indeed, it must be guaranteed for a long period of time. If we are to end up with a government-induced high interest rate policy, the government surely has an obligation to ensure that people have a place to live. It should organize a pattern to ensure that people can borrow long-term money at a fixed rate of interest, on a fixed type of amortization plan.
' I say to Your Honour that this government is proposing to come to this House with an expensive $350 million or $400 million plan. I am not exactly sure what the budget states. It strikes me that if one wanted to reduce interest rates by 2 per cent or 2.5 per cent per year, that would finance $15 billion or $16 billion worth of new mortgage money at a reduction of 2 per cent from, say, 18 per cent to 16 per cent. However, if this government were really interested in doing something, that is the kind of approach it would consider. It would say, "Look, we have to supply long-term plans at a rate which is perhaps less than the short-term treasury bill rate determined by the Bank of Canada's Thursday options."
Second, one would think that if the government wanted to do something, it would say to home owners, "Accept the suggestion of the home builders association." Why does the government not allow people to take their RRSP money, their registered retirement savings plan money, and invest it in their own accommodation?
Right.

Why should people not be able to invest it in themselves? Why should they have to put it with a mortgage company which can then lend it to someone at 16 per cent or 18 per cent interest and all the rest of that nonsense? Why can they not take their own savings money and put it in their houses and, of course, pay taxes on the money when it comes out of their houses when they eventually sell them or when they die? Why can they not take that money and reduce the amount of their indebtedness as a result? Is there anything wrong with investing in real estate, investing in oneself? That suggestion was made by the home builders. There is nothing wrong with it. However, we have not heard that type of suggestion from the Minister of Finance.
What other things can we do? I say to Your Honour that the mortgage tax credit plan which was introduced in the Crosbie budget was a plan which this government should be considering. It certainly has been considered by United Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers in their brief to us from Sudbury. That union clearly came out in favour of that type of an approach to reduce interest rates. It would reduce interest rates in this market by 3 per cent to 4.5 per cent. There are a number of other things which could have been done. But this government's attitude is that housing is a great benefit. It thinks that home owners are making a profit because all of a
Housing
sudden they are part of the tax expenditure plan, that they are costing the government $4.5 billion in taxes because their equity is not taxed, and that because they do not pay rent, which is a benefit, it is somehow not proper and not fair. If you make a capital gain on your home, that is not fair either. If you want to deduct interest over and above the interest you get to develop some real estate or to write off the soft costs you pay to your planner, developer or surveyor, that is not fair. If you want to write off the capital cost allowance, that is not fair because it would make it easier to own and easier to develop rental property. Again there is a tax on, of all things, loans by employers to employees to assist them in buying homes at lower rates of interest than normal. These housing loans should be taxed by the taxman, which would make it more difficult for people to live in a home.
The program of this government and its whole attitude toward housing is repugnant to our society. It is about time the minister looked at this bill and told the Minister of Finance that it is not much of an answer, that the program should be changed in order to come up with something that will attack the housing concerns of Canadians.

But the Government of Canada is not really involved in building houses or financing-
