speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss the bill before us in terms of the supply of affordable rental accommodation in Canada. Hon. members are very much aware of the difficulties encountered by Canadians in many parts of the country in finding suitable, affordable housing to rent. In many of our larger cities, the vacancy rate has dropped below 1 per cent, and 1 per cent vacancy rate means that only one apartment in a hundred is available for rental.
This problem is not a new one. Its origins go back as far as the early seventies when the cost of land, labour and material were rising very rapidly. Rents, however, did not rise at the
same rate, and we found ourselves in a situation in which it was just not profitable to invest in rental construction.
In the mid-seventies, governments, both federal and provincial, intervened. The federal government offered tax incentives and subsidies through the assisted rental program. The provinces brought in rental controls. These measures, together, while providing help and protection for many tenants, prevented the increase in rents which might otherwise have occurred and which would have made rental construction a profitable enterprise.
Since that time, of course, continuously rising costs, coupled with high and volatile mortgage interest rates, have caused a further decline in rental activity. Unfortunately, the scarcity of rental accommodation affects low-income people most severely. Low-income tenants whose rents rise sharply are unable to find alternative accommodation. That is because no reasonably priced housing is being built. Rental investors are discouraged from construction activity because of high interest rates and rental problems associated with competing in a split rental market where older units are rent controlled and newer ones are not.
In these circumstances the people who are least able to compete in the market, such as single parent families, families with children, the elderly and infirm, are hardest hit of all.
The government has approached this problem from two directions. It has taken steps to increase the supply of rental accommodation and it has provided help for those who are most seriously affected by the shortages.
1 know that hon. members are aware of the measures announced in connection with the budget which are designed to improve the situation. The Canada rental supply plan will make interest-free loans available to assist in the construction of 15,000 units across Canada in tight market areas.
In the next two years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The Minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has travelled across the country to discuss the plan with the provincial housing ministers and hear their views as to how the available units should be allocated. The minister told us that some of the provinces were not satisfied with their share of the pie, and his answer to them was very straightforward. He asked them what resources they were themselves willing to set aside to solve the problem. Some of the provinces are willing to supplement the assistance provided under the federal plan through provincial programs. As explained by the minister, the units provided under the Canada rental supply program will give an additional impetus to the rental housing projects undertaken late in 1981 by allowing them to become eligible to use the tax measures concerning the write-off allowed for MURBs. The changes brought about by this bill allow the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, CMHC, to be of greater assistance
February 9. 1982

to the contractors who are willing to take the risks involved in building rental housing in spite of the market conditions. [English]
Because of the rigidity imposed on CMHC by the National Housing Act, as it now stands, the corporation has been unable to be as helpful in financing rental construction as it would otherwise have been. Until now the act has restricted CMHC to charging premiums of 1 Vi per cent or 1 Vs per cent, depending on whether the insured loan is advanced in instalments or on completion of the building.
This rigidity, together with high mortgage rates and rising construction costs, has had the effect of further discouraging builders who contemplated constructing rental accommodation. I am told that at one point when mortgage interest rates reached 21 per cent, CMHC could not insure more than 50 per cent of the loan value of projects being undertaken.
Under current mortgage insurance underwriting practices, an increase of 1 per cent in mortgage interest had the effect of reducing the loan level by approximately 10 per cent. This relationship exists because the single largest item among the operating costs of a rental project is debt servicing. In some cases, for a variety of reasons, some developers are prepared to operate their projects at a loss. However, the risks involved in this type of operation are just too great to be insured with a premium fixed at 1V* per cent.
This is one of the restrictive limitations which this bill would remove. The legislation now before us would delete from Section 5 of the National Housing Act any reference to specific premiums. In future they would be set by CMHC, subject to government approval, at a level which would be commensurate with the actual risks and costs involved. This change would be perfectly consistent with the intention of Parliament when the act was first introduced-namely, that the mortgage insurance fund was to be managed on full cost recovery principles.
This change will give the corporation the flexibility it needs in supporting rental accommodation and all other residential construction to alter its premiums according to changing markets and economic circumstances. More important, this bill will make it possible for CMHC to give more incentives to people who are willing to build such housing. This is in the interest of all those Canadians who are lacking affordable rental housing. CMHC will be able to increase its own levels without jeopardizing the mortgage insurance fund and permit entrepreneurs to get their projects started without having to put up an unjustifiable proportion of capital from their own pockets.
Such a change would not only be in the best interests of CMHC and the building industry but of all those Canadians who, by choice or necessity, rent their homes.
The current rental situation is only one element of the proposed legislation. Now I would like to touch upon the other themes. Before I do, I wish to emphasize just how important the Canadian rental supply plan will be to Canadians all across the country who live in areas where rental housing is in
Housing
short supply or where population growth is expected to take place.
Where is there a surplus?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The plan will help put into place up to
15,000	affordable rental units in target areas of need.
That is just about enough for Scarborough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am thinking of markets in western Canada where the conditions of very low vacancy rates have created housing difficulties. Well known examples of such markets in the west are Calgary, Regina, Vancouver and Victoria.
How about Mississauga?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: I should also add, Mr. Speaker, that these much needed 15,000 units are over and above the 25,000 social housing units which the government is committed to provide in 1982.
That gives us 40,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
These will be provided under CMHC's non-profit and co-operative housing programs. Together, these two federal housing initiatives will produce 40,000 affordable homes for Canadians from coast to coast.
Some amendments may merely seem a dry recitation of technical modifications to an act which has been a major benefit to Canadians since its inception many years ago. But they are much more than that. On the face of it, permitting CMHC to increase its loan levels for the housing industry does not seem to have much impact on the housing consumer. There might not seem to be much connection superficially, but these so-called technical changes will enable those same builders to come into the rental market with units that will be put at the disposal of young and older families and individuals who might otherwise experience serious difficulty in obtaining the housing they need.
The Canada rental supply plan is only one part of the amendments under Bill C-89. The Canada mortgage renewal plan provides important assistance for people who would otherwise incur undue hardship when renewing their mortgages. The government will provide up to $3,000 a year, either in interest deferral or as an outright grant, to home owners who would have to pay more than 30 per cent of their gross income on payments of principal, interest and taxes and 50 per cent of condominium charges.
This is an honest and equitable way to deal with the problem. It targets the help to people who need it and restricts grants in this time of restraints to people who, through no fault of their own, have no equity in their homes.
Other important facets of the bill are the amendments which will enable CMHC to ensure alternative mortgage instruments. Once again this is directed in a very real way to the people of Canada. Potential first time owners have had

February 9, 1982
Housing
problems recently getting into the home owner market because of high interest rates and short-term mortgages. Thanks to the amendments, these Canadians will be able to choose from a broader range of mortgage instruments designed to overcome these difficulties and improve access to home ownership.
I have already spoken at some length on improvements to CMHC's business operations and their importance to the Canada rental supply plan, but I would like to emphasize again that these amendments will have real meaning to individual Canadians. That is why we are here. We are here to put in place policies and legislation that respond to people's needs.
I am satisfied that this bill addresses major issues in housing today, but even this bill is only part of the government's housing thrust. Discussion is well under way on a comprehensive new rural and native housing program, which again will have a major beneficial impact on western Canada. As a longer-term priority, taking into account the need for fiscal restraint, research is continuing into the concept of shelter allowances. The minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has already mentioned these in his own address on this bill. I look forward to further action on these important housing fronts.
1 will wind up my remarks by saying I believe Bill C-89 will enable the government to respond in an equitable and sensitive way to the current issues of mortgage renewals, rental housing, availability and access to home ownership, and I am pleased to support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to begin by saying that as I listenedd to my friend, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael), who has just finished his speech, 1 wondered, coming as I do from the same city, how it was possible for him to make the speech he did, because all the people I talk to and all the things I read indicate that the situation is exactly the opposite to what the hon. member for St. Boniface indicated. 1 know housing prices in Winnipeg are probably less that 50 per cent of prices in cities such as Vancouver or Toronto.
The provincial department of industry and trade puts out a weekly report on various aspects of business life, and one of the items contained in that report every week is a list of the homes in metropolitan Winnipeg which were purchased in a given week two or three weeks prior to the release of the report. I have subscribed to that service for several years, and probably my friend, the hon. member for St. Boniface, also subscribes to that service. For years the list would run six, eight or ten typewritten pages. In the last two or three issues I have received-and I would be happy to show them to my friend, the hon. member for St. Boniface, if he has not seen them- the list has been down to one page. People in Winnipeg are not purchasing homes. They cannot afford to do so. They cannot afford the down payments, and they cannot afford the monthly mortgage payments. When the hon. member for St. Boniface says this bill will help first time home buyers, he is not talking about Winnipeg, and I suggest to him he is not talking about Canada.
The hon. member for St. Boniface also said that the provisions of this bill would take the pressure off people who are finding it difficult to meet their monthly mortgage payments when they come to renewing their mortgages. At some time last summer when the mortgage interest rate escalated from something in the neighbourhood of 12 per cent or 13 per cent to 17 per cent, 18 per cent and, for a period, to over 20 per cent, and when some Members of Parliament from both opposition parties started to ask the minister in charge of housing and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) about how people would deal with this problem, we received replies from both ministers that it was not a very serious problem, that most people who had to renew their mortgages were not having any real problems, that their incomes had gone up, that they could manage, and all that sort of nonsense. I wanted to find out what was happening in my own area, so I surveyed two housing developments in which the houses are probably ten years old or less. I sent questionnaires to residents in those two areas. There were 7,000 homes involved. I assumed, 1 think quite properly, that most people involved in buying houses are carrying five-year-term mortgages. The questionnaire was directed specifically to people who had to renew their mortgages in 1981-82. I calculated that there was a possibility of getting 1,700 replies. 1 could not believe what happened. I was receiving 50 replies every day, and eventually I received over 500 replies of a possible total, as 1 have indicated, of 1,700.
I want to put on the record some of the replies, and I hope the hon. member for St. Boniface and the minister are listening. One of the questions was:
By how much did your monthly payments increase since you last negotiated your mortgage?
One man who replied indicated that his mortgage payments will go up by $300. In the space for comments he wrote:
My wife has had to go to work to make it possible for us to survive. 1 resent having to pay $300 to the bank for absolutely nothing.
Another man said his mortgage payments will go up $333 a month. He said:
Although we won't suffer "hardships" as long as we continue bringing in two full salaries, we cannot afford to start a family-
Another resident's mortgage payments will go up by $300 a month. That resident's comment was:
We are a two-income childless couple. Having old fashioned ideas about a mother staying home to raise her children the increase in our mortgage will certainly decide for us whether to have children or not.
Here is another one:
We purchased a house in April, 1981, and we received a 1416 per cent mortgage for five years, we were very fortunate, now we'll both have to work because we'll need both salaries to pay for the house. After five years we'll decide on whether or not we can survive on one salary-
I will read just one more. This party says that her payments have gone up by $235 a month plus $80. What does the $80 represent? She writes:
The $80 represents A HOP portion which we were promised (documented) a rate of 1 \3A per cent interest but which the federal government is now charging in excess of 21 per cent interest. For an initial loan of $3,690 under the new terms (which are unfair, underhanded and unjust) we must repay over $15,000.
February 9, 1982

I could spend all my time on this because almost every one of these 500 replies contained that kind of comment. Then the minister and the hon. member for St. Boniface tell us this program will help these people.
Now, the minister talked about this great program that the federal government has put into effect that is going to help these people who are caught in this trap. He said to my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) that it was like the Manitoba government program. The minister shakes his head. Yes, that is what he said-and nothing could be further from the truth. Let us just look at it, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: What are the facts?

What does the federal program provide? 1 will put the facts on the record and if I am wrong, the minister or one of his stooges will have an opportunity to correct the record.
What is the federal government's program? It is a program of interest rate deferral. If the interest rate is high, as it has been, they pay two per cent less on their monthly payments than the current interest rate. That is just a deferral. What they have not paid is added to the principal. The result is that the house owner will owe more on his mortgage next year than he did at the beginning of this year. I wish the minister would keep cool. The minister has suggested that people can get up to $3,000 in a grant. Our calculations are that the only people who will get that grant are people who bought homes under the AHOP program-which never should have been developed. They are the only ones who qualify for the grant. They are the only ones who would have less than the 5 per cent equity in their house contract and they are the only ones who would qualify for this grant.
Let us compare that with the program that the Manitoba government put into effect. Their program is not one of interest deferral. Their program is one of direct subsidy, not to the bank, not to the mortgage company, but to the person owning the house and paying for it in his mortgage, and the subsidy can be up to $275 a month on mortgages of not more than $40,000. That is paid if the principal, interest and taxes exceed 30 per cent of the household income.
Let me emphasize again that unlike the federal program, which is an interest rate deferral, which has to be repaid, this is a grant. Home owners who have renewed their mortgages between July 1, 1981, which is about the time when mortgage rates really skyrocketed, and December 31, 1981, will be eligible for up to 24 months of assistance, retroactive to January 1, 1982. Other home owners will be eligible from the time of their next mortgage renewal, and the assistance will be for up to 24 months.
I close this part of my speech, Mr. Speaker, by saying to the minister again that under the Manitoba program the home owners who receive assistance do not have to pay back the amount of assistance that they have received. That is entirely
Housing
different from the program developed by the federal government. The minister may shake his head, but facts are facts. I can tell the minister that I spoke yesterday to two or three people who are leaders in that mortgage action committee, the organization of people who have really been hit by the skyrocketing increase in the mortgage rates, and they are very happy with the Manitoba program. They recognize that the rate of mortgage interest is really the responsibility of the federal government. They regret that the government of Manitoba is going to have to put millions of dollars this year and next year into this program, but they accept the fact that the government of Manitoba is moving in to meet a very important need in a field which is really the responsibility of the federal government.
We have been told that one of the main purposes of this bill is to alter the terms and conditions under which mortgage insurance is offered to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We have been told that this is one more way of getting more funds into the mortgage market. Every time a change is made to the National Housing Act, which relates to mortgages, the argument has been made that the change is necessary to make mortgage money available through the lending institutions. What do we see and what is the record in connection with this argument?
What we have seen is the 6 per cent ceiling on national housing mortgages removed in 1967. The requirement that mortgages be set at no more than 2% points above long-term government bonds was removed in 1969. Mortgages were supposed to go down to less than 9 per cent as a result. There has not been a mortgage rate below 9 per cent since then. The roll-over term in mortgages was introduced in 1973 to enhance the attractiveness of mortgages as an advance. Before that we had 25-year mortgages. We are told that we would have five-year mortgages that would really induce the lending institutions to put more money into the market. Now we are being told that we cannot have five-year mortgages, that we should have one-year mortgages. In fact, we are told that we should have mortgages that change every time the bank interest rate changes.
New mortgage rates are being introduced in this bill, the variable rate mortgage in which your rate changes every time mortgage rates go up. Under today's conditions this means that the mortgage rate could roll over every week when the bank rate changes. This will eliminate risk to the lender who presumably puts the money into the market. It also allows for more interest deferral. The changes in mortgage insurance will encourage the use of these vehicles.
There was a time when a mortgage was a debt which people incurred with full knowledge of what they were getting themselves into and what the total payment would be.
The people who replied to my questionnaire said they thought in 1975 and 1976, when the interest rate was between 11 per cent and 12 per cent, that they had a pretty fair idea of what they would be paying for all the years that they were paying for the house. Five years later they were getting the kind of increases to which I referred.

February 9, 1982
Housing
In today's market, in the way the government proposes to set it up, there is no way of determining how much the person would have to pay or how long it will take him to pay off the debt on the house. The provision for mortgage insurance on all these risk instruments which the government is proposing moves Canada ever closer to the permanent debtor society.
As my colleague says, they are AEIOPing all houses-as if we have not had enough bitter experience of that disaster.
In allowing the insurance to determine the premium totally based on the risk factor, the people who can least afford the extra cost, that is, the home purchaser, will be asked to shoulder it, and the lender, who has better insurance cover for any risk he takes, will be encouraged to exercise even less discretion in providing it. Since second mortgages can also be insured, insurance will probably become a requirement for these loans, adding more costs and encouraging more people to get into debt way over their heads, which is exactly what happened when we adopted the AHOP program.
Who is going to benefit from this? Not the home owner. The people who are going to benefit from this are the banks. Let us just look at what is happening to the banks. In one year, between 1980 and 1981, bank profits went up by 37.7 per cent. The Bank of Montreal profit in 1980 was $263 million; in 1981 it was $358 million. The Toronto-Dominion bank profits went up from $182 million in 1980 to $255 million in 1981. The profits of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce rose from $192 million to $310 million in 1981, and the profits of the Royal Bank rose from $327 million in 1980 to $492 million in 1981. This was a total increase of $500 million in one year. This is the kind of money we require in order to build the housing units we need.
It was bad enough that the banks experienced tremendous increases in profits. It was even more insulting that the Liberal government allowed banks to get away with tax rates as low as 9 per cent in 1981, which was lower than the tax rate of people earning under $10,000. The average tax rate for the five largest banks in 1980 was 15.3 per cent, a paltry amount compared with the 50 per cent rate of a decade ago. If banks had paid taxes at normal corporate rates of 46 per cent, they would have paid $650 million to the federal treasury rather than paying approximately $225 million. The government wonders where to get money from; this is one area.
We in the New Democratic Party have a couple of proposals for the government and the minister. First, we propose a windfall profits tax to regain lost tax dollars banks should have paid. Second, it is time the government did what many governments in the western world have done, that is direct banks to set aside a portion of their loan portfolios for reasonably priced mortgages. Instead of such a program, we see a disastrous housing program which will exacerbate the deplorable situation in which many Canadians live.
It has been estimated that the housing needs of the country would be met if we constructed approximately 220,000 housing units this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: With the help of the NDP government of Manitoba?

The NDP government of Manitoba will look after itself. It will have to account to the people of Manitoba four years from now on its record. I have more confidence in the ability of that provincial government to be re-elected than I have in the ability of the present Liberal government, especially if it does not change its policies.
Rather than meeting that need, the projection for housing starts this year is somewhere between 145,000 to 165,000. A report in yesterday's paper indicated that housing starts for January, 1982, were at an all-time low. In 1979 there were
197,000	housing starts; in 1980 they dropped to 158,000, the lowest figure since 1966; in 1981 there were 178,000 housing starts. This figure will decline very substantially in 1982.
Hopefully we will receive these 160,000 housing starts, which is the top estimate, but what would be the effect if we built 220,000 units? If an additional 60,000 units were erected this year, it could involve an additional 120,000 jobs for construction workers, electricians, plumbers and construction material manufacturers. It would put some of the thousands of laid-off forest workers back to work. It would create a market for appliances so that the lay-offs, about which I asked the Minister of Finance earlier today, would be obviated, such as 800 people in an appliance plant in Montreal who were laid off last Friday. It would give some hope to the people who manufacture appliances, television sets, radios and plumbing supplies. These would be some of the results of an active housing program. These additional homes could be targeted as social housing. It would involve an additional $500 million expenditure to the Canada Mortgage and Housing budget. As I have already indicated, the funding for this could come from the windfall profits of the banks in 1981.
1 take this opportunity to say to the minister that I am bitterly disappointed with the failure of the government to begin programs which would lead to the construction of new housing units and with its failure to bring forward programs to help stop the rot of the core areas of most Canadian cities. Such a program would permit people to remodel, refurbish and rehabilitate tens of thousands of homes, the quality of which has been reduced in the last 25 years. I am referring to houses in the core areas of Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Calgary and Vancouver from where we have seen an exodus of people. These are areas in which the schools, streets, sewer, water and power systems have been built and paid for. People are moving out of these areas to the suburbs. Schools in these core areas have been closing, while new schools costing tens of millions of dollars have been built and are being built in the suburbs. Why are people moving from these areas? It is partly because of the age of the homes and because the conveniences they expect to find in homes in the 1980s are different from what they were in the 1920s and the 1930s. We should have had for a long period of time, for at least ten to 20 years, very aggressive housing rehabilitation programs.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Like the one we have in Winnipeg?
February 9, 1982

Like the one they are beginning again in Winnipeg. There was no need for these people to move to the suburbs. Years ago they paid from $20,000 to $50,000, and in recent years $100,000 or more, when homes which had been built years earlier could have been rehabilitated and brought up to present-day standards for a fraction of the cost. But the Liberal government was not prepared to say to the provinces and the municipalities that it was willing to co-operate and share in the funding of such programs.
This brings me to a program of which I am very proud. The new NDP government of Manitoba announced that it was reinstituting and starting at a much greater pace a program which was in place from 1969 to 1977, its critical home repair program. Under the program, pensioners will receive grants of up to $1,500, and low and moderate-income Manitobans who occupy their own homes will receive up to $3,000 in combined loans and grants. The premier announced that the program was established as a successor to the highly successful pensioners' home repair program. During those eight years some
19,000	homes were repaired at a cost of $17 million, of which some 14,000 homes were repaired as a result of applications made or approved during the 1975 to 1977 period.
Under the new program, here are some of the guidelines. The income qualification ceiling for pensioners has been increased from $10,000 to $14,000. A maximum $1,500 grant, not a loan, is available to those with an income of $7,000 or less. A sliding scale provides $1,100 for those with incomes of $9,000 to a minimum of $100 for those with incomes of $14,000. The government of Manitoba has increased the income qualification ceilings for families from $10,000 to $16,000. The income eligibility is adjusted to take into account dependants. Where adjusted income is $10,000 or less, a family is eligible for a $700 repayable loan at a fixed subsidized rate and the optional low interest repayable loan of $900 has a potential total of $3,000. The Manitoba government has increased the maximum potential grant for pensioners from $1,000 to $1,500. The government has increased the maximum potential grant or loan for low-income families from $2,000 to $3,000. The Manitoba government has reduced the effective interest rate for loan repayment to a fixed subsidized rate of 9.5 per cent over eight years from 14.5 per cent.
This is what the government of Manitoba did. This is a have-not province, whether it has a Progressive Conservative government or a New Democratic Party government. The government will not solve the housing problems of the city of Winnipeg, but the government is at least making a start and it is helping people who need assistance to rehabilitate the kinds of homes found in the core area of Winnipeg which need so much improvement.
I wish that the federal government, which has so much more ability to plan and fund these kinds of programs, would start something of that nature.

It would have to clean house first.
Housing

Let me deal with just one more point. I wish that the government would reconsider the disastrous decision it made a year and a half ago to suspend and end the community services contribution program. That program replaced three earlier programs, the neighbourhood improvement program, the program to help municipalities fund sewer and water extensions, and another program.
When the minister announced the ending of other programs and announced the establishment of the community services contribution program, he said that it was designed to provide sewer and water systems, non-profit housing and improvements to neighbourhood facilities.
In a very short period of time, because of this insane insistence of the government that expenditures have to be reduced, that program which the minister announced with such great fanfare was ended. The program was created in 1978 to fill the gap left by three other improvement programs which were snuffed out by the government. It started out with a lower budget than the budget for the three programs it replaced. But the government committed itself when the same minister whom we have now committed the government to funding the new program for five years. Two years later into the program the minister said that the projects that had already been started would be funded to completion, but no more money would be provided to replace the community services contribution program.
What that meant for the city of Winnipeg was a very serious block in its plans to rehabilitate the older part of the city. Federal funds totalling over $12 million were made available to the city of Winnipeg for a project carried out between January 1, 1979, and December 31, 1981. Unfortunately, there will be no more funding of any projects after this year. With the federal government deciding not to replace the program, what we will have in Winnipeg and in other cities is a significant increase in the rate of unemployment and an almost complete stoppage in the plans to rehabilitate those areas which are seriously run down in Winnipeg, about which I know the most.
What we have had from this government and from this minister since the government took over has been retreat after retreat and stoppage after stoppage. As I have indicated by quoting from some of the replies I received to the questionnaire I sent out, this has put tremendous pressure on people who purchased homes in good faith five or six years ago. An almost complete stop has been put to plans of cities to rehabilitate their core areas. A virtual halt has been put on purchases of new homes. I do not have time to go into this, but we are seeing virtually the end of the building of rental accommodation, whether in the private or in the public sector.
When the minister prides himself that he is providing funds for the building of 15,000 rental housing units, he is not even talking about meeting the needs of one city, let alone meeting the needs of the whole country.
All of this disaster that I have recounted in the field of housing is only part of the picture. We see this kind of halt put to essential improvements in almost every phase of life of

Canadians. We see it because the government, although it has not quite adopted the whole range of Reaganomics, has adopted the essential part of Reaganomics, and that is the idea that no matter what cost to people and to necessary institutions, somehow the deficit in government expenditures must be halted.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We have not adopted their deficit.

The Minister of Finance has said that this situation is temporary, that the economy is going to get moving in the United States some time this summer and automatically the Canadian economy, which is so closely geared to the American economy, has to pick up. One only needs to read a newspaper such as The New York Times to see how false that hope is. The President of the United States, that great conservative, who spent 20 years telling the American people that government deficits were a disaster, and if only he were elected he would do away with government deficits, is telling the American people that next year the deficit will be $96 billion. That is if the American Congress accepts the very sharp cuts in social welfare which the president proposes. If the Congress does not, and in an election year it is not likely to then they will be talking about a deficit of over $100 billion. The American government will have to go to the market to borrow the money. When the Americans do that, they will be competing with the needs of the private sector. The inevitable result of that will be an increase in interest rates in the United States and in Canada, since the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance have adopted a policy that Canadian interest rates shall be locked in with those of the United States. Therefore, we will be facing increased interest rates in this country. That, Mr. Speaker, will be a disaster for home owners, renters, in fact all the people of Canada. That is the inevitable result of this government's housing policies.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in the debate this evening and to be able to follow the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), or perhaps "the hon. member for a disaster about to take place" would be the more appropriate designation. I found it interesting in the extreme that he can see nothing but disaster, and that caused me to reflect just a moment, Mr. Speaker, that we as Canadians, all in the same boat as he professes to be in tonight, would have such a pessimistic outlook on the future of Canada, indeed of ourselves as individuals, as to make us all seek some kind of professional help to try to get up and out of these doldrums.
I would love to be proven wrong.

1 just cannot perceive that anyone with so little optimism for the future could hope to be in fact representing those who sent him here. I hope those who are more optimistic about the future of Canada than he professes to be will write him and tell him that they do have a little optimism notwithstanding what he says here.
I would also like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that he was quick to try to characterize the concepts and precepts promoted by this government by calling them Reaganomics. Yet, for some strange reason, he seems to be able to make the jump- by not having the kind of deficit forecasting that exists over there, the $96 billion at best and over $100 billion at worst- and criticize this government for allegedly following Reaganomics, and miss the fact we are not proceeding in that direction of deficits which he finds so abhorrent.
You are worse.

I do not know how one can be on both sides of that chasm except that perhaps it is not a chasm, perhaps it is a fence and he is in the unfortunate position of being on both sides at the same time, which has the unfortunate consequence of being incredibly painful. Perhaps that is why he is so pessimistic tonight.
A beautiful night.

I wish to support Bill C-89, Mr. Speaker, a bill to amend the National Housing Act and the CMHC Act. I think one of the overlooked undercurrents in this debate has been the constant and responsible manner in which CMHC has performed its duties. I wonder how many other organizations have had the same record of excellence over the past 35 years. Perhaps it would do us some good to review the events for a moment.
Mortgage insurance was introduced in Canada by CMHC in 1954, and in fact the Government of Canada has been helping Canadians since the 1930s to fill their housing needs by making sure there is an adequate supply of mortgage money. CMHC emerged in the waning years of World War II. In its earliest years, when it was known as Central Mortgage and Housing, it administered joint public and private mortgage loans, although mortgage insurance did not come into effect until the mid-1950s.
The mortgage insurance fund was financed with premiums paid by borrowers, and it pooled the risks involved in mortgage investment. In addition, CMHC made direct mortgage loans in many parts of Canada where private loans were not available. When the MIF was established it was intended to be totally self-financing. Premiums were set at a level which would be enough to offset any claims which could be reasonably met. Of course, the fickle finger of fate, if I may describe it as such, caught up with this scenario. An unprecedented rise in claims created a liquidity problem for the fund since its accumulation of marketable securities was depleted and most of its assets were in real property, which CMHC had accepted in settlement of claims.
More important, there was a problem of solvency. Currently, the premiums which CMHC can charge for mortgage insurance are set out in the National Housing Act and cannot be adjusted except by an act of Parliament. This is one of the reasons why these changes to the National Housing Act must be made, so that CMHC can operate in a more businesslike approach. It is essential to the well-being of CMHC.
February 9. 1982

It has already been stated that the bill before this Parliament would allow CMHC to adjust mortgage insurance premiums, set them at a level appropriate for the risk involved, and sufficient to cover the cost and expenses of doing business. This arrangement would allow CMHC to insure new, innovative mortgage instruments which it could not cover under the fixed premium system. The CMHC application fee has never been really adequate to cover the shortfall out of operating revenues. They have been covered primarily out of surpluses which have accrued from its own direct loans to builders and home owners. I must say, in supporting this bill, that I find the CMHC approach to doing business to be totally responsible. This is evident in the amendments before the House.
The bill would in large measure correct this shortfall by permitting CMHC to charge application fees appropriate to the costs. In short, the fund would be self-sustaining. Furthermore, any surpluses accruing after costs and expenditures . would be retained by the fund. This is only good business practice and would enable CMHC to undertake the normal business practice of setting aside surpluses in the good years to provide for any future deficiencies.
Keep in mind that the current legislation under which CMHC conducts its insurance business was framed and evolved in an extended period of relatively stable growth and low inflation. Times have changed, Mr. Speaker, and these changes to the act are responses to current realities. It is clear that the changes will make CMHC more responsive, more in tune with what is happening in the business and housing world.
There is a tremendous amount of resourcefulness in industry in this country. I firmly believe these changes will allow CMHC, in the housing sector, to play an important role in responding to the challenges of the eighties. There is no shortage of great ideas in the private sector. As a result of these changes, it will allow government to perform an essential supportive role, heretofore prohibited under the restraints of the old NHA. The changes are all intertwined: The terms and conditions under which CMHC may insure mortgages, the way it may charge for that insurance and the methods by which it may settle claims on these mortgages.
It is disappointing that some hon. members opposite cannot fully grasp the significance of these amendments which will allow CMHC to be more responsive and responsible. If it paid any heed at all to the comments from the other side, the government would have to spend probably billions of dollars on housing. And where will the money come from? The taxpayer, by whatever means. The members opposite must have some unshared wisdom about some untapped source of cash. When will they learn that the role of government, as has been amply demonstrated by this government, is to be both responsive and accountable to the people, the taxpayers of Canada?
Take, for example, the statements made in the House yesterday about the rental housing situation. A prime example of this, Mr. Speaker, is the Progressive Conservative housing critic's comments about the current rental housing situation. The hon. member seemed to be implying that the government was not meeting its responsibilities with respect to rental
Housing
housing. Unfortunately, he was quoting out of context a document which was made public some months ago. Repeated attempts were made by the government to explain that the analysis of the rental housing situation in the document was based on a "worst case scenario".
I should like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it was in order to discharge this very responsibility that the scenario was drawn up. It permitted the government to review all options carefully and to propose the Canada rental supply plan, which is designed to put some 15,000 affordable rental units into place in the coming months. It is an equitable and responsible program, and indications from the development industry have confirmed a general support for the thrust of the program.
It is interesting, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member complains that the rental supply plan is inadequate to meet all rental housing needs. In making that comment, we should all remember that the hon. member speaks for the same political party which would have privatized CMHC and diminished dramatically the federal government's role in providing affordable housing for all Canadians. 1 think emphasis should be drawn to that last statement. It should not be overlooked by this government.
There was also criticism that there had been no meaningful discussion with provincial housing ministers. During my time in the House since 1974, how many times have I heard that over and over again? One begins to wonder how one defines "meaningful discussion", and what it means to hon. members who, in fact, claim it has not taken place. Does it somehow mean that in order to have a meaningful discussion one must adopt the position of the opposite party? Is that meaningful discussion?
That's what you guys do all the time.

In any event, whatever the definition, the claim and criticism is that there has been no meaningful discussion with provincial housing ministers. Once again, it seems to me that this demonstrates that the members of the opposition have not been listening. If they had been listening, they would have heard the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) say that he had travelled across the country to discuss the principal components of the proposed amendment to the National Housing Act. As a matter of fact, it might be worth while to quote the minister who indicated that he had discussed the legislation and that he was generally pleased with the response he received. The minister said:
In my conversations with them I have emphasized that housing, in Canada, is a shared responsibility and that the provinces, as well as the national government, have a role to play in providing access to housing and particularly in responding to local needs and local priorities.
1 am happy to say that, in some cases, the provincial governments are responding to the federal initiative and are developing programs which would be compatible with the Canada rental supply plan.
The federal government's initiative, combined with ongoing social housing programs, has been welcomed, as a contribution to the alleviation of a serious problem. I have given them the assurance that the available resources may be reallocated during the year if it is found that one region is not taking up all of

February 9, 1982
Housing
the assistance that was designated for its use and there is an urgent need elsewhere.
I ask Your Honour, reflecting on what the minister has said, can a reasonable man conclude in any way, shape or form that there has not been discussion, that there has not been reflection on the issue and that there has not been a meaningful discussion with the provincial ministers? Even so, the claim is made.
I believe that Bill C-89 is a positive response to a number of problems confronting Canadians today. I have not gone into detail about the Canada mortgage renewal plan because it has already been covered in some detail by previous hon. members. However, once again, the renewal plan is an example of a program which is tailored to real need and to the need for restraint. No one in this House wants to stifle debate or worthwhile suggestions which could help to improve the supply of affordable housing. Indeed, it has frequently been suggested that we would not only be pleased to accept any good idea but that we would also adopt it and, if pressed a little, give credit to the author. However, that does not seem to be the purpose of what is going on in the House today. It seems, rather, to be simply criticism for criticism's sake, and that is unfortunate.
Improving access, supply and home ownership security is what this bill is all about; but unrealistically expensive and unworkable proposals which go against current thinking and the current economic and fiscal situation can only serve to delay implementation of sensible and targeted programs which would be of real benefit to Canadians across the country.
I commend the provisions of Bill C-89 to hon. members opposite. For the sake of both home owners and renters from coast to coast, I hope that there will be no undue delay in obtaining passage of the amendments.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the House, before I begin my remarks I would like to announce the passing of one Daisy Graydon, who was the widow of the former leader of the Progressive Conservative Party and a former member of Parliament, Gordon Graydon, the former hon. member for Peel, which constituency he represented from 1935 to 1953. I know that two of my colleagues, the hon. member for Brandon-Sou-ris (Mr. Dinsdale) and the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) sat with Mr. Graydon in this House. I know we all pass on our sympathies to the family and friends of Daisy Graydon.
I welcome this opportunity to speak on the subject of housing and the issues facing the Canadian housing market today and to discuss Bill C-89. It is a sad commentary on what we are going through today, but I have in my hand a bumper sticker which I came across just recently. It states, "I live in this car. Trudeau took my house". It is a shame that that type of thing has to be seen in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Laugh!

Hon. members opposite think it is funny. Canadians often debate whether housing is a right or a privilege. Over the last year, we have seen the dreams of many home owners shattered and the aspirations of would-be home owners destroyed because of the failure of our economy and destroyed because of inflation and the high cost of money.
The present interest rate policy and the approach of this government in taxing the low and middle-income Canadians to the point where they have barely enough left to exist, and its approach to inflation, all contribute to a situation in housing which has reached crisis proportions, whether the government will admit it or not.
Most Canadians dream of owning their own home. That dream is being turned into a nightmare for some and a distinct impossibility for others. Everyone needs a place to live. Whether what we call home is a rental unit, an apartment, a single family dwelling or whatever, depends on our needs and means, but having a place to call home gives us security and roots. Whether we own or rent, the issue facing each of us is affordability. Some of the stories which have been told in the House over the last couple of days of debate are very true. A family in my riding has now doubled up. They have lost their home and have moved in with their parents. They are facing a very bleak time right now. I know of a couple earning $18,000 a year. The man drives a car and is now being taxed $3,800 for the privilege of driving that car. That raises his income and puts him in a different income bracket. He has just refinanced his home, but he cannot afford the payments any longer because of the new tax bracket which this government, with its inept budget, has put him into.
The shelter costs for a great many of us represent the largest, most important expenditure we make. Given the importance of housing to each of us, and given the fact that housing represents a basic right of all Canadians, how can this right be ensured by government? I believe and can honestly say that this government has done nothing to ensure affordable housing. It has done nothing to spur housing starts but has done just the opposite. It has eliminated any incentive builders may have had. However, being an optimist, I can say that it is not too late for a reassessment of our interest rate policy. I urge those Liberals with the courage to stand up for what was formerly the great Canadian dream to do so.
The current policies of this government are damaging every job-creating sector in this country. The Canadian residential construction industry was a healthy, viable concern until the last couple of years. Roughly 5 per cent of our labour force is dependent on this industry for jobs. The industry has no incentive to construct moderately priced ownership and rental housing. It is not constructing this kind of housing because it is being destroyed by high interest rates and by economic conditions as a whole. Two years ago, there were some 7,500 builders in Canada. Today, only 3,500 still survive, and that number is going down every day. If we look briefly at our population growth, the impact of our record low housing starts becomes very evident. Our population has grown tenfold in the last 130 years. Our over-all population growth has never been

February 9, 1982
lower than 1 per cent. In my riding alone, the growth rate has been roughly 10 per cent per year over the past five years.
I would like to speak briefly with regard to a particular segment of the housing problem in my riding of Brampton-Georgetown. However, to really do the subject justice, I would like to refer to the Peel region as a whole.
The Peel regional government makes up the communities of Caledon, Brampton and also of Mississauga. It is under the chairmanship of Frank Bean who presides over close to half a million people. It represents a perfect example of the unwillingness of this government and its lack of foresight and planning.
As we all know, the federal government implemented AHOP. The minister refers to it as "a hope". Some say, no. It was implemented in 1973 to encourage construction of affordable new housing. When it was introduced, AHGP represented a major shift in federal housing policy. Previously CMHC had been concerned with supplying mortgage funds. AHOP was CMHC's first attempt, some hope it is their only attempt, to offer direct ongoing cash subsidies to home buyers and, oh boy, it failed.
The perils of AHOP in Peel have been and continue to be brought to the attention of the minister responsible for housing. However, until recently it would appear that the loopholes of AHOP have been of no great concern to him and his government.
The AHOP fiasco was foreseen by the Peel region, by the member of Parliament from there, and should have been seen by CMHC, but no one at the federal level could admit that there were problems with the government's panacea to housing shortages.
Jim Crozier, the commissioner of social services in Peel, made representations many times to the minister. AHOP owners groups made many representations to the minister over the years, and he did not listen. He did not listen until very recently.
When AHOP began, the rapid growth rates between 1971 and 1980 and available land made Peel a prime location for developers building under AHOP. In 1971 the population of Brampton was 70,838. In June, 1981, it was 148,150, an increase of over 100 per cent. The Peel region saw an increase of 79 per cent in that same period.
A large part of the AHOP problem was that too many AHOP units were built in Peel too soon. Inducements brought in buyers that should not have reasonably been expected to be buyers, and the ethics of the matter left much to be desired. This was discussed in the House many times.
Although AHOP did increase demand among families otherwise ineligible for home ownership, this subsidized demand was not enough to absorb all the AHOP units. The glut of AHOP housing had profound short-term effects on the retention of value.
Housing
Because of the imbalance of supply and demand in Peel, gimmicks to market the units were used; one dollar down payments, five month free rent options, low mortgage rates. Many of the people attracted to AHOP, 73 per cent, were young, first-time buyers. Closer credit screening would have saved many dreams. The real estate value of AHOP units created another problem. Values of many homes actually depreciated, and 1 know that to this day there are still units being sold under their original mortgage value. The ethics of the efforts of the developers and government to attract virtually any low-income family can be questioned. They had a responsibility. They did not live up to it.
Current figures show that 55 per cent of Peel's AHOP units have had their titles returned to CMHC as a result of foreclosure, issuance of power of sale or quit-claim deeds. That is 55 per cent, and the minister says this program is a success. The dreams of all these people have been shattered.
The number of AHOP units on CMHC's books constantly changes. There may be more coming on this year when people remortgage their homes. Currently CMHC has title to 527 units in my area. Of this, 351 are high rise and 176 are row. Last year 50 to 75 units per month were being returned to CMHC. What will it be this year? We do not yet know.
It was the AHOP issue and the dedicated work of people such as Jim Crozier and Marlene Grant that brought to light our serious housing problems. People became concerned, fearful, and began feeling helpless about the whole housing issue. The minister started to take note when they began banging at his door in Scarborough. He then realized that maybe something was wrong in this country.
Something that concerns me is that this system put these people into the homes. The system also kicked them out and shattered their dreams. When this happens, people rebel against the system. I do not want to see, and I know the minister does not want to see, people rebelling against the system, but when the system does that, it follows.
I would like for a moment to address a point repeatedly made by my friends in the NDP concerning the defaulted AHOP units. The solution put forward by that party over the last year, and by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) was to turn the vacant AHOPs into rental units. That sounds like a very commendable solution. However, it does not take into consideration the realities of the real estate market.
Home owners who had their hard earned savings invested in the purchase of their units became very concerned that the vacant units might be turned into rent-geared-to-income units. They were concerned about the retention of the value of their homes or about trying to get the value back to what they originally paid for it. If statistics can be believed, they had every right to be concerned.
Rent-geared-to-income units should not be proposed in ownership projects. Market values dictate that the ownership and rent-geared-to-income projects be kept separate, unless it is a co-op housing development.

February 9. 1982
Housing
In Bill C-89, which we are debating, the minister responsible for housing has finally seen fit to introduce legislation to pass the meagre assistance to home owners facing mortgage renewals. I sat through his speech yesterday. It was interesting to note his comments on the $3,000 grant being offered. What he failed to mention was the fact that very few people will be eligible to take advantage of this grant because the regulations are so severe.
This government grant does not begin to solve the mortgage renewal problem. What it does, I am afraid, is to postpone the inevitable. It will make those few who are eligible dependent on Ottawa for the very roof over their heads, a dependence which is very dangerous when one considers the philsophy of this government and its irresponsibility.
The minister's comments yesterday were of some interest. I wondered how he could stand in his place and say that the amendments in this bill will permit young families to buy their first home. That is beyond me. Is this bill going to lower the interest rates? Is this bill going to change our real estate market trends geared, because of economic conditions, to second and third time buyers who have existing equity? No. Mr. Speaker. It was enlightening to hear the minister for the First time admit that there has been a financial drain in the CMHC fund because of high AHOP defaults.
What is infuriating is that we on this side of the House have been asking for action for two years. It has taken this government two years to become, as the minister says, sensitive and concerned about the problem. Those are empty words. For people facing an escalation in shelter costs, there is very little good news, and this bill certainly gives none.
Returning to the role of the government ensuring our rights to housing, the erosion of real income and the escalation in shelter costs have shut out the vast majority of young people who are in search of accommodation. If the minister's riding is like my riding, I am sure that he has had young people coming to him every day of the week to ask how they will be able to afford a home or where they can rent an apartment. The fact is that these accommodations are just not available. The severe shortage of affordable rental accommodation no longer makes renting an alternative. By the end of 1982 there will be an estimated shortfall of 1,517 rent-geared-to-income units in Peel alone. The fact that these units are needed by families and senior citizens may not be of any concern to the minister but it is of great concern to me and to my constituents because if these shortfalls continue we are headed for severe hardship in my particular area of Canada and I know in the minister's area as well.
The minister stated that part of the $350 million for housing which was included in the now infamous budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will finance the rental supply plan over the next two years. We need 1,500 units right now in my riding alone. We do not need them tomorrow, not by the end of 1982, but right now. That is the waiting list. It is a legitimate waiting list.
The stimulus to construct 15,000 units over the next two years across Canada is quite infinitesimal, but it coincides with everything else the government is doing. For example, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) stood up and said, in answer to a question today about high interest rates, that the government gave $25 million to some group that is going to create thousands of jobs. We know that is not true, knowing the cost of creating one job.
Now this minister is throwing a little here and there-they are all doing it just to say, "Are we not great? We are doing something." But they are not really doing anything.
I sat here yesterday and listened to a number of Liberal members talk about the Progressive Conservative proposal for mortgage interest deductibility and property tax deductibility program. I think it is time that we dispelled some of the myths that the government constantly enjoys creating. My hon. friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Peterson), stood in his place yesterday and had the audacity to state that our proposal would have been unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: To renters.

I will come to that, Mr. Minister. According to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice, a deductibility program for any type of expense always benefits higher income taxpayers. I would suggest to him that the realities of paying a mortgage do not solely belong to higher income earners, something which may be a revelation to members opposite because they are all high income earners. Most people who have mortgages are not rich. I invite the hon. member to tell the young families in my riding who are struggling to pay their mortgages that they are rich. I invite the hon. member to come to Bramalea and to the villages of Heart Lake where it is the ambition of young families-who would benefit greatly from a deductibility program-to pay off their mortgages, to tell them that they are rich. These families make up the majority of my riding. I ask the hon. member to tell them that they are rich.
The rich have always had the same deductibility benefit which the Liberals consider unfair for middle and low-income earners. The proceeds from a mortgage are invested, and the interest has always been a tax write-off, and still is to a limited extent, of approximately $10,000 a year. Would it be unfair to renters?

In answer to the minister, his government introduced the measure which enables the owner of the rental unit to deduct mortgage interest as a business expense. They have always had that privilege. This has helped to keep rents lower than would have otherwise been the case if deductibility was not available to the owner.

That is a scam.

I would also like to tell the parliamentary secretary that, with regard to those people who are renewing three or five-year mortgage plans who, according to him, have experienced significant increases in equity, equity does not mean a thing unless that property is sold.
I would like to reiterate that if what is contained in Bill C-89 is all that the government is willing to do or to propose to alleviate some of the problems facing us, then let us get on with it.
At this point 1 would like to congratulate the minister.
Hear, hear!

I am thankful that the minister has stayed in the House during the full debate. That is a rare occurrence with this government. He is to be congratulated for that. As a matter of fact, I feel sorry for him because I genuinely believe that he does have some concern for the home owners, but I think that the Minister of Finance and his cabinet colleagues have hung him out to dry.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Have you read the Matthews report?
That is three years old. Why do you not do something?

The provisions in Bill C-89 are not adequate. It will not encourage adequate housing starts. People who are renewing mortgages are not adequately assisted, and the rental accommodation shortage is not adequately addressed. However, it is obvious that the meagre aid in Bill C-89 is all that Canadians will get. The government has been too slow in attaching any significance to the housing question. When you add the housing situation to the economic picture, the lack of confidence in this government which is evident across Canada is very understandable. Nothing could serve the

national interest more than a few resignations by members opposite.
