subtopic: TRADE-(A) IMPORTATION OF LIGHT TRUCKS (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: TRADE-(A) IMPORTATION OF LIGHT TRUCKS (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I rose last week to ask the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) a question regarding the importation of small Japanese trucks, I was only touching upon a small part of an extremely large problem. Two questions during our daily question period cannot address the real problems facing our automobile industry. The question put to the minister is symbolic of the whole problem. Let me be a little more specific and you will see the dimensions of the problem.
When the Japanese ministry of international trade and industry wrote to our Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce on June 4, 1981, an understanding on a quota was reached with respect to automobiles. We agreed to increase our quota by 10 per cent over the 1980 import totals. The Americans negotiated a 6 per cent decrease in their import totals of Japanese automobiles. Light trucks were not part of our quota consideration and, as a result, light truck imports increased 122 per cent over the previous year.
Three of our domestic manufacturers have introduced light trucks comparable to those imported from Japan. We are presently levying a tariff of 12.9 per cent on imported trucks. That tariff is due to decrease to 9.2 per cent under a GATT agreement which we have signed. When we look at the American action in this field, we see that the Americans levy a 25 per cent tariff, and they do not intend to reduce that tariff under the GATT agreement. In other words, they are going to take a tariff protection route for the domestic manufacturers of small trucks.
My point is that with domestic production under way in North America in light duty trucks, does it not make sense to have a quota and a stabilized duty of even 12.9 per cent? If we

February 9, 1982
Adjournment Debate
do this, we will assist our domestic production in getting a foothold in the marketplace. To do otherwise would add to a problem which is already out of hand.
We have only had one year of surplus since the auto pact was signed. Each year our balance of payments in the automotive account has been in deficit and is growing and growing by gigantic leaps and jumps. The standard reply that 50,000 jobs have been created is what we usually hear from the minister. However, with the downturn in the industry, many of these jobs are now becoming redundant. The pressure for change in the auto pact has been building for a number of years.
A few years ago the government decided to hire a consultant to review the auto pact and to make recommendations. The government employed Simon Reisman, a former deputy minister of industry, who was one of the architects of the original auto pact. Naturally, Mr. Reisman found little wrong with the agreement he helped put into place. I recall attending a meeting with Mr. Reisman at which he simply put down anyone who was critical of the auto pact. Even at that time we could see the tremendous disruption which was taking place in our balance of payments. Of course, after listening to Mr. Reisman, I left in disgust.
A very large part of our current account deficit is tied up in the automobile industry. We are dumping more and more money into a variety of programs, only to see them fall apart down the road. It is this type of patchwork approach we have to stop. We must review the whole matter with a sense of urgency.
I see a decline in the manufacture of heavy duty trucks in Canada; this spells trouble for the transportation of goods down the road. It is just not attractive to become an investor in the automobile industry today, and yet we see a pent-up demand building which is being held up by high interest rates. 1 am not convinced that the minister, his department and the government are really aware of the size of the problem facing us.
If the negotiators meeting with the Japanese do not insist on a quota for light trucks, my statements will prove to be correct. A realistic look at the auto pact over the last 18 years shows that in the early stages our Canadian content was 58 per cent. In 1981 that slipped to 56 per cent. In other words, after 18 years of involvement in the auto pact, Canadian content propped 2 per cent rather than going up as it should have.
We are a mobile society. The automobile, the light truck and the heavy duty truck will be with us for as far as we can see ahead. I want the minister to tell us when we will begin to .address this very, very serious problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE-(A) IMPORTATION OF LIGHT TRUCKS (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to my good friend, the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling). Let me first look at the reality. Japan is one iof our main trading partners. In 1980 we exported $4,345,.474,000 worth of goods to Japan and imported from Japan $2,791,516,000 worth of goods. In other words, we sold a little over $1.5 billion worth of goods more to Japan than we
imported from Japan. If there is a complaint, it is a complaint from Japan's side that we are not purchasing more from Japan.
The figures are deceiving. I have carried the hon. member's figures through somewhat. His thesis is that because we do not have the 25 per cent tariff the United States has-our tariff is only 12.8 per cent-that is damaging and we should do what the United States has done.
Two years ago, and we are talking about mini-trucks specifically, the Japanese had six per cent of our market. Last year they had 11 per cent; and this year, in this short period, it is 16 per cent. That is, with a tariff of 12.8 per cent. The tariff in the United States is double that amount; it is 25 per cent. Yet for the last three years the Japanese share of the United States market has been 20 per cent. With double tariff, they have a larger share of the United States market.
We are now concerned. Earlier this year we reached an agreement on passenger cars with the Japanese, that from April 1, 1981, to March 31, 1982, they would not export more than 174,213 cars, to Canada.

subtopic: TRADE-(A) IMPORTATION OF LIGHT TRUCKS (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION
speechtext: That is 10 per cent above the 1980 basis, it is not light trucks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE-(A) IMPORTATION OF LIGHT TRUCKS (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION
speechtext:
It does not include light trucks, that is right. But General Motors is now in the mini-truck business, and I hope their truck is productive. I find it humorous to hear a spokesman for that great party of the free enterprise system here in Canada telling Canadians that once again we should protect American companies operating in Canada, the three of them, because they are not operating productively.
I spoke to a superintendent of U.S. Steel on Sunday about the car market and he said that with inflation going down and interest going down, hopefully, we still have the problem on this continent, especially with U.S. Steel, that the Japanese are manufacturing their automobiles and trucks at $10 U.S. per hour and the Americans are manufacturing theirs at $20 U.S. per hour. You cannot blame all that on labour. This involves an attitude, a matter of reinvesting in modernized equipment. More tariffs, as the hon. member has suggested, create more subsidy to inefficiency. I note that my time is up. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a very high regard for the men and women in Canada's Armed Forces. I feel that they fulfil their function admirably and under considerably great difficulty. I have a high regard, too, for the gentleman who is our Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne), who was himself a gallant soldier. I feel that Parliament's function is to indicate to our Armed Forces the role that we want them to perform and then to give them the personnel and the material to fulfil that obligation. It is in
February 9, 1982

supplying the Department of National Defence with the personnel and material that I feel we are not fulfilling our function adequately as parliamentarians. Tonight I would like to indicate some constructive measures that I hope we can consider in fulfilling that obligation.
It is my opinion that our Armed Forces are understaffed and underequipped because they are underfinanced. In 1963, 24 per cent of Canada's budget was allocated to the Department of National Defence. This year 8.6 per cent of our budget is so spent. In 1963 we had 120,000 men and women in our Armed Forces, and today we have 80,000. In the year
1980-	81 we budgeted $5.04 billion for national defence and in
1981-	82 we will increase that to $5.9 billion.
Over the years our increases in real dollars when stripped of the inflation factor, barely meet 3 per cent requirement of NATO. We are at the lower edge of prudence in that regard. I think we met that requirement this year, thanks to the expenditures for new fighter aircraft.
Speaking of our new fighter aircraft, we expect the first copy of the 137 F-18A Hornets to be available this fall, probably in October. Two years ago when we signed the contract for this fighter aircraft-and it is badly needed-we felt that the estimated cost would be $2.3 billion. Right now the estimated cost is $5 billion. This increase in cost is certainly not entirely the fault of the Department of National Defence, but it raises some question which I think we should address about the viability of the management process and ongoing re-equipment planning in terms of the Armed Forces.
It has been 11 years since we have had a white paper on national defence. It is just about time we took a look into the future, did some planning and had another one. In the army component of the Armed Forces we have trucks which are older than the drivers. This is the situation in regard to much of our mobile equipment. We have 19 tanks stationed in Canada and the rest are with NATO in Europe. These 19 tanks are barely enough for training purposes. The Leopard tank, about which I am speaking, is an excellent tank, but its numbers are so small that it can fulfil very few functions. We have received reports that in western Canada some members of the Armed Forces exist on welfare. I should like to see the report rebutted, and I hope the opportunity to do so will be taken tonight when the parliamentary secretary replies to this allegation.
Our navy has four 280 Tribal class destroyers. These are efficient and can give good account of themselves. The other grand old ships of the line are regrettably just about 30 years old. They can get the steam up when their boilers are not cracked, but they have to stay pretty well within hailing distance of ports because of their advanced age. The St. Laurent was sold two years ago. While it was being towed down south to be junked, the towline broke and the St. Laurent sank; that is the sad story of our navy. We have four Oberon class submarines, three on the east coast and one on the west. They take their turns being patched up because they are 20 years old. The one on the west coast is in dry dock most
Adjournment Debate
of the time. We have six frigates in the definition contract stage. This contract was varied or altered once. I cannot say with reliability when they will come on line, but I can say that they are very badly needed.
What will we do about the situation? It will cost a tremendous amount of money to purchase new equipment. Canada has very extensive shoreline in the north, on the east and on the west. We have a small population with a limit to what we can raise in revenue, as well as tremendous demands on our dollars.
My suggestion is that we should take a page out of World War II experience, when we had an excellent lend-lease program with the United States of America, and that we rent or lease equipment from the Americans. What about our sovereignty? Can we do this and maintain our sovereignty? What about Canada's defence industry and our superior training methods? Will the Americans be interested? We will never know until we ask them, but 1 think the answer would be affirmative because the Americans have been our friends in peace and our allies in war. They know our economic situation and our limitations. We supply the defence for their northern frontier. They have large amounts of equipment and a tremendous budget which will be increased. The amount for which we would lease from them would be infinitesimal. If we enter into a contract to lease from them, we can protect our sovereignty and perhaps receive some spin-off benefits in terms of defence construction for Canadian industries. I notice my time is almost up. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and my colleagues, for your indulgence.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Ursula Appolloni (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the surface the idea of leasing military equipment as proposed by the hon. member would appear to have some merit, at least in theory. In practical terms, however, this is an option that has not normally been entertained for a variety of reasons which I will try to outline.
There is an interdepartmental committee under the chairmanship of the Treasury Board secretariat that studies instances wherein leasing could constitute a desirable means of satisfying certain facility and equipment needs. Unfortunately, in the case of military equipment, the Department of National Defence has no knowledge of any such modern equipment, compatible with Canadian requirements, that is available for lease. While it is entirely possible that upon investigation some equipment could be found it is most probable, however, that the owner nation would have already discarded such equipment as being either too old, beyond the state of economic repair, or requiring considerable modernization to make it capable of contemporary utilization. I am sure the hon. member does not want us to be second cousins to anyone in the military department.
In most cases, modern equipment not actively in use by owner nations, is normally required by these nations as reserves in time of war and it is unlikely that they could be

February 9, 1982
Adjournment Debate
made available for long-term lease. In general terms, it can safely be said that the equipment must fit the task to be performed.
Certainly, this is very relevant to the point made by the hon. member in his original question in which he said that we had only 19 Leopard tanks in Canada. On this point, I would like to correct him by informing him that we have 43 tanks in Canada.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: Not in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: In Canada.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: The rest are in Europe.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I gave the hon. member the courtesy of my attention. Surely he can reciprocate. Even as a Tory, he might have some good manners.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: Try to be accurate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBILITY OF LEASING EQUIPMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
More important is the point that tanks do not have a significant part to play in any of the defence of Canada scenarios. If we do have tanks at Gagetown it should be clear that they are for the training of the armoured personnel who will man our Leopard tanks stationed in Europe where they do have an important operational task.
The question of Leopard tanks is more interesting in some other aspects, and I can understand the hon. member basing his question on the fact that we did, a few years ago, rent that type of equipment from our German allies. But we must put this matter of the tanks in the correct context. The short-term leasing of Leopard tanks made imminent good sense because we were getting that very type of equipment in our own inventory shortly thereafter.
A factor that is not readily understood and one that is omitted from the member's comment is the fact that the rental of equipment itself is only one very small part of the total defence equation. Ancillary questions that must be considered include the retraining of operations and maintenance personnel, additional spare parts and support equipment requirements, the compatibility of current ammunition holdings, and, most important of all, the capability of the equipment to fulfil the task at hand.
I see that my time has run out, although I could have gone on at length, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: subtopic

NATIONAL DEFENCE-(A) COMMITTEE STUDY OF CANADIAN FORCES BASE CHATHAM, N.B. (B) MINISTER'S RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 8, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) confirmed that the U.S. F-18 Hornet fighter plane will not be based in Chatham, New Brunswick, but instead will go to Cold Lake, Alberta, and Bagotville, Quebec. He confirmed that the squadron presently based in Chatham will be phased out and, indeed, the existence of the air base itself has become
very much in question. The personnel that are based there will be transferred or laid off, as the case may be. That announcement was made on November 8, 1981.
By December 15, the minister had used the typical ruse of this government of giving the air base a reprieve. He postponed the replacement of the fighter squadron until 1984. We have seen this sort of thing happen several times. It is part of the old syndrome of "Boys, we will rip your head off'; only to hear then, "Don't worry, fellows, we don't really mean that, we are just going to break your legs".
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) did the same thing when he talked about indexing pensions and other things which would have had a severe consequence to some of our pensioners. When it ended, it was just an ugly rumour and it wasn't really going to happen at all, but he would not close the door to it. This seems to be the way this government operates, and that is a little disconcerting to say the least.
The minister met with the leaders of the region during the latter part of December and assured them there would be some things happening in Chatham. He would not be specific but said there was going to be something in Chatham to alleviate the base closure. He said he would get back to them in January or February and in the meantime was going to set up an interdepartmental task force made up of various deputy ministers from however many departments were involved, and said they would report to Parliament by the end of January. They were going to be charged with the responsibility of making suggestions as to what they were going to replace that base with.
On February 3, Mr. Speaker, after telling the minister I wanted to know what suggestions the task force had made and what suggestions he was going to make to cabinet, I asked the minister:
Will the minister now tell the House what recommendations that committee has made?
The minister's response was:
Madam Speaker, the answer is yes.
What kind of a response is that, Mr. Speaker, to a quite explicit question? I simply asked if the minister would tell the House what the committee's recommendations were and he answered:
Madam Speaker, the answer is yes.
Then he went on to explain that Canada's security was well taken care of, which is not at all what I asked him. After I reminded him of that, he did indeed respond in substance, because I believe he was embarrassed into some kind of response that at least alluded to the fact that I had asked the question.
Let me just give you a brief history of the role of this base in Chatham. It has in the past played a very important role in the defence of Canada in the Atlantic Coastal Canadian Identification Zone. We are told by National Defence people that
February 9, 1982

there is an increase in Russian Bear aircraft travelling in this zone.
Mr. Speaker, you point to your watch; 1 would just like to confirm that I do have seven minutes, and I have used three of them now.

speechtext:
As I recall, Mr. Speaker, I got on my feet at 10.20. But at any rate, let me simply say that this base plays a very important role. The minister will say that they are moving the F-18 aircraft to Bagotville because it can take care of the northern regions of Canada which must come under scrutiny as well. Let me tell the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, in case he does not know it, Chatham is located at a more northerly position in this hemisphere than is Bagotville. In addition, it is farther east and is therefore closer to the identification zone and certainly in a much better position to identify these aircraft.
We also have a very important situation in that over 3,500 people will lose their jobs in the Chatham area. That will mean the loss of $25 million or $30 million in wages and an additional $12 million in lost spin-offs.
The people at Chatham are looking for replacements. They are looking to this government to do something about the situation in which they find themselves. They are concerned, and they have every right to be concerned. I have asked the Minister of National Defence to tell the people of Chatham, in specific terms, what replacement for the air base he will recommend to his cabinet colleagues. I have asked him to assure those people who will lose their jobs, and their families, the townsfolk of Chatham and the businessmen of the community who will be greatly affected by this closure that, indeed, the government will be taking specific, positive steps to ensure that all of that lost income will be replaced, as the minister and the government has suggested in very, very general terms. I expect that the assistant to the minister will now be very specific and will answer the question.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Ursula Appolloni (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-(A) COMMITTEE STUDY OF CANADIAN FORCES BASE CHATHAM, N.B. (B) MINISTER'S RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I would like to emphasize to hon. members present, and especially to the people of the Miramichi region, that the decision to locate the eastern operational base of our new fighter aircraft, the CF-18 Hornet at Bagotville, was taken with the best military and strategic intelligence available. A thorough analysis of all basing postures was completed before a final decision was reached.
In the context of protecting Canadian sovereignty in the military sense, of course national defence would have preferred to operate a larger number of bases, thus ensuring adequate overlap of air defence coverage. However, when all factors were weighed and considered, it became necessary to compromise in certain areas.
Adjournment Debate
There were three main factors considered in our deliberations with regard to the selection of the best location for our bases: peacetime sovereignty; threat and air defence considerations and, of course, cost.
In the initial stages of the program, operational research staffs completed a detailed study of all basing operations and detailed comparisons were made among the various options identified.
